problems.title: Some antibiotics
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (11 points). Some antibiotics

The Austrian company Sandoz GmbH with their factory in Tirol is the largest producer of antibiotics and the only real producer of penicillin in the western world. The company accounts for approximately two-thirds of the worldwide production of penicillin V, the acid stable penicillin that was discovered in 1951 by two scientists from Kundl.

This penicillin V as well as three other antibiotics provide a small insight into the synthetic paths in organic chemistry.

A. Prontosil

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-1-fig1.png

Hint: $\mathbf{B}$ shows signals in the molecule peak reagion at $m/z = 233$ and $m/z = 235$ in a 3:1 ratio.

1.1. Draw the constitutional formulae of the compounds $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, and benzene-1,3-diamine.

1.2. Why is the step $\mathbf{E}\to\mathbf{F}$ impossible when benzene is used instead of benzene-1,3-diamine?

1.3. What type of stereoisomerism can occur in $\mathbf{F}$?

B. Chloramphenicol

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-1-fig2.png

1.4. Draw the constitutional formulae of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and the configurational formulae of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

1.5. Draw the structural formulae of the reactive species in the reaction $\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{E}$ and name the respective reaction mechanisms.

1.6. Name substance $\mathbf{C}$ according to IUPAC.

C. Trimethoprim

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-1-fig3.png

Hints:

• Substance $\mathbf{B}$ has the name 3,4,5-trihydroxybenzenecarboxylic acid methyl ester.
• Substance $\mathbf{E}$ is a mixture of isomers.

1.7. Draw the constitutional formulae of the compounds $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ and write down the molecular formula of $\mathbf{X}$.

[The answer boxes are labelled A, B, C, D, E and X.]

Guanidine (reactant of $\mathbf{E}\to\mathbf{F}$) is surprisingly basic $\mathrm{p}K_B = 0.35$.

1.8. Which effect in protonated guanidine is responsible for this fact? Draw at least two structural formulae in order to show this.

D. Penicillin V

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-1-fig4.png

1.9. Draw the configurational formulae of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

problems.title: Birch sugar
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (4 points). Birch sugar

Monosaccharide $\mathbf{A}$ is a xylose. This name derives from the Greek word for wood and indicates the occurrence of this sugar in bark (wood sugar). A modified substance (xylitol or birch sugar) is found in birch trees. Xylitol has won relevance for diabetics as a sugar replacement (E 967).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-2-fig1.png

Hint: Substance $\mathbf{F}$ is idose and is name according to IUPAC is (2S, 3R, 4S, 5R)-2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal.

2.1. Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{F}$ in Fischer projection.

2.2. Draw the two pyranose sugars $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$ formed in the Haworth projection and name both monosaccharides.

2.3. Name the special isomeric relationship between $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$.

2.4. Draw the structural formula of the disaccharide in the Haworth projection that is formed through the combination of $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$. This substance shows a negative reaction wit Fehling’s solution.

problems.title: A journey through the world of metals
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (9 points). A journey through the world of metals

In the Lavant Valley, mining is about to be expanded with a focus on metal $\mathbf{Y}$. There is a binary inorganic compound $\mathbf{Z}$ ($M = 45.88\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) of metal $\mathbf{Y}$ with an oxygen/metal ratio of 1:1, containing 69.75% oxygen.

3.1. Determine which metal the mentioned metal $\mathbf{Y}$ is and provide your calculation below.

This type of metal can bind oxygen anions as $\ce{O^{2-}}$, $\ce{O2^{2-}}$ and $\ce{O2^{-}}$.

3.2. Write down the exact total formula of substance $\mathbf{Z}$.

The metal $\mathbf{Y}$ has a density of $\rho = 0{,}534\,\mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}}$ and crystallises into a lattice with $a = 351\,\mathrm{pm}$.

3.3. Calculate into which cubic lattice the metal $\mathbf{Y}$ crystallises.

One possibility to gain the metal barium is the reduction of barite (barium sulphate) with carbon. Amongst others, a chemical compound containing carbon in the oxidation state +IV is produced. The produced metal sulphide is then reprocessed with water and carbon dioxide. The resulting salt is annealed. The hereby resulting metal compound is transformed with aluminium into the metal and aluminium oxide.

3.4. Write down balanced reaction equations for the four discussed processes.

The metal oxide $\ce{BaO}$ crystallises into a sodium chloride structure type.

3.5. Specify the coordination numbers of the metal and oxide ions in the crystal structure.

Barium forms several oxides. Some selected examples are $\ce{BaO}$, $\ce{BaO2}$ and $\ce{Ba(O2)2}$.

3.6. Write down balanced reaction equations for the formation of the three metal oxides from their elements.

When discharging ozone into a solution of the metal barium in liquid ammoniac, a sepia brown, extremely labile metal ozonide should be formed. Ionic ozonides are vigorously decomposed by water under the formation of oxygen. The resulting solution is alkaline.

3.7. Write down the balanced reaction equation for the reaction of the ozonide ions with water. Assign oxidation states to all atoms.

For the secure storage of large amounts of hydrogen (e.g. for operating a fuel cell) metal hydrides can be used. An example for such a metal hydride is $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$. It is gained by mixing (“ball milling“) magnesium hydride and elemental nickel.

3.8. Calculate the amount of hydrogen in $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ in percent by mass.

Simplified working hypothesis: The nickel atoms are arranged face-centred cubic in the unit cell of $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ and the Mg-ions fill the tetrahedron gaps. Around each nickel atom four hydrogen atoms are coordinated.

3.9. Draw all nickel atoms (without H atoms) as coloured balls, and one magnesium ion, which you can choose freely, as a triangle into the given unit cell. Indicate the tetrahedron for the chosen magnesium ion with dashed lines.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-3-fig1.png

3.10. How many tetrahedron gaps and how many octahedron gaps are there per unit cell?

3.11. Write down the amount of formula units of $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ in one unit cell.

The metal hydride is examined by X-ray diffraction. The diffraction of the first order at the (111)-plane occurs in an angle of $11.92^\circ$ when $\mathrm{CuK_\alpha}$-rays are used.

3.12. Calculate the lattice parameter $a_0$ of the unit cell.

3.13. Calculate the density of $\ce{Mg2NiH4}$ powder in $\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

Problem 4 (6 points). Something „Gschmackig’s“(= tasty) from Tyrol

A. The „Tiroler Zelten“

The following ingredients are necessary for the preparation of a tasty „Tiroler Zelten“: 375 g rye flour, 375 g wheat flour, 500 ml lukewarm water, 20 g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp caraway, 1 tsp fennel, ½ tsp aniseed, ½ tsp cilantro, 1 egg for brushing and halves of almonds for decoration.

The molecule $\mathbf{W}$, which can be found in the dough for the „Tiroler Zelten“, comprises 70.56% C, 5-93% H – the rest is O. The mass spectrum of substance $\mathbf{W}$ is given as spectrum 1.

spectrum 1:

A combustion analysis of $2.9644\,\mathrm{g}$ of substance $\mathbf{X}$ results in $8.8020\,\mathrm{g}$ $\ce{CO2}$ and $2.1624\,\mathrm{g}$ $\ce{H2O}$. The molar mass of substance $\mathbf{X}$ is $M < 200\,\mathrm{g\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

Approximately 50 years ago, Robert Sidney Cahn, Sir Christopher Ingold and Vladimir Prelog published an article titled “Specification of Molecular Chirality” in the renowned scientific journal Angewandte Chemie. It was a comprehensive illustration of the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog system and about to change chemical terminology by introducing the term of chirality. Problem 5 (10 points). The A to G of Nickel Complexes

This task is about several nickel complexes, their structure, their reactions, their ligands. Each complex is assigned a letter as an identifier as can be seen in this overview

• $\mathbf{A}$: $\ce{[Ni(NH3)6]^{2+}}$
• $\mathbf{B}$: $\ce{[Ni(NO2)6]^{4-}}$
• $\mathbf{C}$: $\ce{[Ni(OH2)6]^{2+}}$
• $\mathbf{D}$: $\ce{[Ni(NH3)2(OH2)4]^{2+}}$
• $\mathbf{E}$: $\ce{[Ni(en)(OH2)4]^{2+}}$
• $\mathbf{F}$: $\ce{[Ni(en)3]^{2+}}$
• $\mathbf{G}$: $\ce{[Ni(CO)4]}$

5.1. Hereunder some names of complexes are given. If you find some of the ones specified above, fill in the corresponding letter. (Note: Whereas there will be no negative marks for this part of the task in total, wrong answers will lead to deduction of points.)

• hexaamminenickel(III) _____
• hexaaquanickel(II) _____
• hexaethylendiaminonickel(II) _____
• hexanitratonickel(II) _____
• diamminetetraaquanickel(II) _____
• tetraaquaethylendiaminonickel(II) ______
• tetracarbonylnickel(II) _______

Let us now take a closer look at the three octahedral complexes $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

5.2. Write down the complete electron configuration of the central atom in these complexes.

5.3. Draw a diagram showing the splitting of the d-orbitals of Ni in the octahedral complex. Decide which magnetic properties you expect.

For the complexes $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ values of $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$ have been measured. You can find them in the following table in different units of energy.

problems.title: Bombastic Calorimetry
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (5 points). Bombastic Calorimetry

In this task all data given and asked for are referred to standard conditions .

Two isomeric, liquid hydrocarbons ($\ce{C8H8}$) have been investigated: cycloocta-1,3,5,7-tetraene and styrene = vinylbenzene = ethenyl benzene. They were burnt in a bomb calorimeter with an excess of oxygen so that $\ce{H2O_{(l)}}$ and $\ce{CO2_{(g)}}$ were formed. Ignition was achieved by means of a wire whose heat of combustion in both cases was $Q_\mathrm{wire} = -30.0\,\mathrm{J}$.

The lab assistand carrying out the experiments labeled the samples “A“ and “B“, conducted the measurements, wrote down the results and then left for lunch. On his return, however, he unfortunately had forgotten which substance actually was “A“ and which was “B“.

The lab journal showed these data:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{compound} & \text{initial weight } m/\mathrm{g} & \text{heat measured } Q/\mathrm{J} \\ \hline \text{A} & 0.7834 & -34181 \\ \hline \text{B} & 0.6548 & -27623 \end{array}$$

Also known are $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{H2O_{(l)}}) = -285.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{CO2_{(g)}}) = -393.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

6.1. Give a balanced equation for the combustion including the symbols for the states of matter.

6.2. Calculate the molar standard enthalpies of combustion $\Delta_\mathrm{c}H^\circ$ of A and B.

6.3. Calculate the molar standard enthalpies of formation $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ$ of A and B. In case you did not get a result in 6.2. use $\Delta_\mathrm{c}H^\circ_\mathrm{A} = -4581\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{c}H^\circ_\mathrm{B} = -4431\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

6.4. According to the standard enthalpies of formation, one of the substances should be more stable with regard to dissociation in the elements than the other. This is… (tick the right circle!).

• compound A
• compound B

6.5. According to Hückel’s rule one compound is aromatic. Into the brackets write the number of $\pi$-Elektrons of the ring systems and mark the aromatic compound.

• cyclooctatetraene (____)
• styrene (____)

6.6. Assign which compound was which sample by correctly filling in A or B respectively.

______ was cyclooctatetraene ______ was styrene

It is possible to estimate enthalpies of combustion using a so called incremental system. Therefore it is assumed that a certain bond or a certain group of atoms in the gasphase gives the same contribution (an increment, $\Delta_\mathrm{c}H_\mathrm{I}^\circ$) to the enthalpy of combustion regardless of its chemical surrounding. For every substance the enthalpy of evaporation or of sublimation has to be added to the sum of increments.

As an example the calculation for cyclooctatetraene is shown:

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta_\mathrm{c}H^\circ &= 8\cdot\Delta_\mathrm{c}H_\mathrm{I}^\circ(\text{C-H}) + 4\cdot\Delta_\mathrm{c}H_\mathrm{I}^\circ(\text{C-C}) + 4\cdot\Delta_\mathrm{c}H_\mathrm{I}^\circ(\text{C=C}) + \Delta_\mathrm{c}H_\mathrm{I}^\circ(\text{Ring}) + \Delta_\mathrm{vap}H^\circ = \\ &= 8\cdot(-226.1) - 4\cdot(206.4) - 4\cdot(491.5) - 4.2 + 43.1 = \\ &= -4561.5\,\mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-6-fig1.png

Enthalpy of evaporation: $\Delta_\mathrm{vap}H^\circ(\text{styrene}) = 43.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

6.7. For styrene calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion according to the incremental system.

By its very basic assumption (always the same contribution of energy independent of surrounding) the incremental system completely disregards stabilizing effets such as resonance (mesomerism) or delocalization, wich are substantial for aromatic compounds.

6.8. For both hydrocarbons calculate the stabilization energy through a comparison between the calculated and the measured enthalpies of combustion.

problems.title: A kinetic mixture
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (7 points). A kinetic mixture

A. Nitrogen oxides

An important step in the technical synthesis of nitric acid is the oxidation of nitrogen oxide to nitrogen dioxide with the aid of oxygen from air:

$$\ce{2 NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2 NO2(g)}$$

The reaction obeys the following kinetic law: $v = k\cdot[\ce{NO}]^{2}\cdot[\ce{O2}]$

7.1. Put a cross into the box where the factor of the change in rate matches the concentration change.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \rlap{\text{The rate changes with the factor}} & & & & & & & & \\ \text{Change of concentration} & 1 & 2 & 4 & 8 & 16 & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{4} & \tfrac{1}{8} & \tfrac{1}{16} \\ \hline [\ce{O2}] \text{ quadrupled, } [\ce{NO}] \text{ unchanged} & & & & & & & & & \\ \hline [\ce{O2}] \text{ unchanged, } [\ce{NO}] \text{ quadrupled} & & & & & & & & & \\ \hline [\ce{O2}] \text{ unchanged, } [\ce{NO}] \text{ halved} & & & & & & & & & \\ \hline [\ce{O2}] \text{ halved, } [\ce{NO}] \text{ quadrupled} & & & & & & & & & \\ \hline [\ce{O2}] \text{ quadrupled, } [\ce{NO}] \text{ halved} & & & & & & & & & \end{array}$$

The initial rate of the above reaction remains the same, if the temperature is raised from $460\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and the initial concentrations are halved.

7.2. Calculate the activation energy of the reaction.

B. The iodation of acetone

Measuring the rate of a chemical reaction and its dependence on several parameters (concentration of involved species, temperature, pressure, and catalysts) enables the chemist to draw conclusions about the reaction mechanism and thus about the detailed way of the reaction.

In compulsory lab lessons at a Viennese High School the iodation of acetone under acid catalysis is investigated:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-7-fig1.png

The reaction does not proceed in one step, but in several ones, one of them being the rate determining step (RDS).

The rate equation of the reaction is given:

$$v = -\frac{\Delta[\ce{I2}]}{\Delta t} = k\cdot[\mathrm{Ac}]^{a}\cdot[\ce{H3O+}]^{b}\cdot[\ce{I2}]^{c}$$

The students have to mix various volumes of the involved reaction partners, knowing their initial concentrations. Additionally they have to measure the time until the colour of iodine disappears, therefore

$$\Delta[\ce{I2}] = [\ce{I2}]_0 - 0 = [\ce{I2}]_0.$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-7-fig2.png

Reaction flask at the beginning (or during) and at the end of measurements (“t am Ende” = t at the end) [Footnote: Foto: Manfred Kerschbaumer]

The values of four experiments are given in the table below. The volumes refer to the stock solutions of the following substances which were mixed to a final volume of $20.0\,\mathrm{mL}$:

$c(\ce{I2}) = 0.0101\,\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$; $c(\ce{HCl}) = 1.96\,\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$; pure acetone ($\rho = 0.790\,\mathrm{g\cdot mL^{-1}}$);

Immediately after the addition of acetone the stop clock was started. When the solution first got colourless the clock was stopped. The corresponding times are also given in the table.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{try} & V(\ce{H2O})\ \mathrm{mL} & V(\ce{HCl})\ \mathrm{mL} & V(\ce{I2})\ \mathrm{mL} & V(\mathrm{Ac})\ \mathrm{mL} & t \text{ in s} \\ \hline 1 & 7.0 & 8.0 & 3.0 & 2.0 & 39.3 \\ \hline 2 & 11 & 4.0 & 3.0 & 2.0 & 80.1 \\ \hline 3 & 8.0 & 8.0 & 2.0 & 2.0 & 26.0 \\ \hline 4 & 7.5 & 8.0 & 3.0 & 1.5 & 53.0 \end{array}$$

7.3. Calculate the amount of acetone in 1.00 L (= „concentration of Ac“).

7.4. Fill the missing values into the table, calculation the individual initial concentrations and the reaction rates of the four experiments.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{try} & c(\ce{H3O+})\ \mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}} & c(\ce{I2})\ \mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}} & c(\text{Aceton})\ \mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}} & v \text{ in } \mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}\cdot s^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & & & & \\ \hline 2 & & & & \\ \hline 3 & & & & \\ \hline 4 & & & & \end{array}$$

7.5. Write down an equation for the differential reaction rate of the iodation of acetone using the right integer reaction orders.

7.6. Calculate a mean value of the rate constant with the right units.

7.7. Put a cross (crosses) left of the reaction equation which corresponds to a possible RDS which matches the differential rate law..

[The four printed reaction equations, one per row of the table:]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-7-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-7-fig4.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-7-fig5.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2016-7-fig6.png

C. The Rice-Herzfeld-Mechanism

Radical chain reactions often show a very complex differential rate law. In some cases, however, relatively simple equations appear. One example is the pyrolysis of ethanal to methane and carbon dioxide.

The differential rate law for this process is given:

$$\frac{d[\ce{CH4}]}{dt} = k_{EXP}\cdot[\ce{CH3CHO}]^{\frac{3}{2}}$$

In the year 1934 F. O. Rice and K. F. Herzfeld were able to explain this more or less simple law by using a complex mechanism. Their proposal was four elemental steps:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{Start:} & \mathrm{CH_3CHO} \rightarrow {}^\bullet\mathrm{CH_3} + {}^\bullet\mathrm{CHO} & k_a \\ \text{Propagation:} & \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + {}^\bullet\mathrm{CH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_4} + \mathrm{CH_3CO}^\bullet & k_b \\ \text{Propagation:} & \mathrm{CH_3CO}^\bullet \rightarrow {}^\bullet\mathrm{CH_3} + \mathrm{CO} & k_c \\ \text{Termination:} & {}^\bullet\mathrm{CH_3} + {}^\bullet\mathrm{CH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_6} & k_d \end{array}$$

7.8. Write down a balanced equation for the pyrolysis reaction.

7.9. Write the formulae for the unstable particles of the propagation reactions into the two boxes.

7.10. Proof the differential rate law given above, assuming a steady state mechanism for the unstable particles of the propagation reactions.

7.11. Write down a relation between $k_{EXP}$ and the rate constants of the elemental steps.

Problem 3 (7 points). Aluminum and Complexes

Aluminum crystallizes in cubic closest packing of spheres and can be described as fcc aluminium. It has a density of $\rho = 2.699\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Nowadays aluminium can be rolled out to foils reaching thicknesses of $0.004\,\mathrm{mm}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2017-3-fig1.png

3.2 Calculate the lattice parameter $a$ in pm.

Aluminum is easily soluble in hot concentrated hydrochloric acid, forming $\ce{[Al(H2O)6]^{3+}}$ ions. At room temperature, aluminium can be dissolved in strong bases and forms $\ce{[Al(OH)4]^-}$ ions. Hydrogen is released in both cases.

3.3 Assign the correct systematic names to the ions formed during both processes:

$\ce{[Al(H2O)6]^{3+}}$ Name:

$\ce{[Al(OH)4]^-}$ Name:

Bauxite is an important raw material for the production of metallic aluminium. This aluminium ore consists of aluminium oxide-hydroxide $\mathrm{AlO}_x\mathrm{(OH)}_{3-2x}$. ($0 < x < 1$)

In order to convert bauxite into sufficiently pure aluminium oxide, the Bayer process is used. At higher temperatures, sodium hydroxide solution is added to bauxite, whereby aluminium hydroxides easily dissolve leaving behind undissolved residue, "red mud". Typical, industrially used bauxites contain $\ce{SiO2}$, $\ce{Fe2O3}$, $\ce{TiO2}$, $\ce{P4O10}$, etc. besides $\ce{Al2O3}$.

$$\ce{Al2O3} + \ce{OH-} + \underline{\qquad} \longrightarrow \ce{[Al(OH)4(H2O)2]-}$$

$$\ce{SiO2(OH)2^{2-}} + \underline{\qquad} \longrightarrow \ce{CaSiO3 v} + \underline{\qquad}$$

$$\ce{[Al(OH)4(H2O)2]-} \longrightarrow \underline{\qquad} + \ce{OH-} + \ce{H2O}$$

$$\ce{Al(OH)3} \longrightarrow \ce{Al2O3} + \underline{\qquad}$$

Consider a rod made of ruby that is $15.2\,\mathrm{cm}$ long and has a diameter of $1.15\,\mathrm{cm}$. It contains a mass fraction of 0.050% (m/m) $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ ions. The so-called iodine clock experiment shows the kinetics of a reaction in a classical manner. Two colourless liquids are mixed and after a short time the solution turns blue. There are different versions of this experiment. In one of them is the following reaction important:

$$\ce{S2O8^{2-} + 3 I- -> 2 SO4^{2-} + I3-} \qquad \text{(All species dissolved in water.)}$$

The following mechanism has been proposed for this reaction:

$$\ce{S2O8^{2-} + I-} \xrightarrow{k_1} \ce{IS2O8^{3-}}$$

$$\ce{IS2O8^{3-}} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{2 SO4^{2-} + I+}$$

$$\ce{I+ + I-} \xrightarrow{k_3} \ce{I2}$$

$$\ce{I2 + I-} \xrightarrow{k_4} \ce{I3-}$$

5.9 Derive an equation for the rate of formation of $\ce{I3-}$. Use the steady state approximation for all reaction intermediates.

C. Electrochemistry of sulfur compounds

A Latimer diagram for a series of sulfur species at pH = 0 is given. All potentials are given in Volt:

$$\ce{HSO4-} \xrightarrow{\quad x \quad} \ce{S2O6^{2-}} \xrightarrow{+0.569} \ce{H2SO3} \xrightarrow{\quad y \quad} \ce{S2O3^{2-}} \xrightarrow{+0.600} \ce{S} \xrightarrow{+0.144} \ce{H2S}$$

[Below the chain, two further arrows are printed: one from $\ce{HSO4-}$ to $\ce{H2SO3}$ labelled +0.158, and one from $\ce{S2O6^{2-}}$ to $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$ labelled +0.456.]

5.10 Calculate the missing potentials x and y.

5.11 Prove by calculation that S(0) is stable against disproportionation.

5.12 Provide a balanced equation for the disproportionation of S(II) with the species indicated in the Latimer diagram.

5.13 Calculate the equilibrium constant for this disproportionation at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Hydrogen peroxide can occur as an oxidizing and reducing agent. The standard potentials are given:

$\ce{O2}/\ce{H2O2}$ $\quad E^\circ = 0.69\,\mathrm{V}$ $\qquad$ $\ce{H2O2}/\ce{H2O}$ $\quad E^\circ = 1.77\,\mathrm{V}$ $\qquad$ $\ce{S2O8^{2-}}/\ce{SO4^{2-}}$ $\quad E^\circ = +1.96$

5.14 Does hydrogen peroxide react with $\ce{Na2S2O8}$ under standard conditions as a reducing or as an oxidizing agent? Tick the correct answer.

• reducing agent
• oxidizing agent

5.15 Write down the correct redox equation and calculate $\Delta E^0$.

problems.title: Lead, Calcium and Equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (7 points). Lead, Calcium and Equilibrium

In an aqueous solution from a technical process, both calcium and lead(II) ions are present.

In the course of quality assurance, the metal ion concentrations normally determined by ICP-OES are to be controlled by a wet-chemically method using complexometric titration with EDTA.

$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ can be titrated against methylthymol blue with EDTA at pH = 6 under the conditions specified in the analytical specification, and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ does not react at first. The concentration of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ is determined in the same (titrated) sample at pH = 12 against the same indicator. According to the operating procedure, $25.00\,\mathrm{ml}$ of the liquid to be analyzed are first transferred to a titration flask. Dilute nitric acid, the indicator methylthymol blue and solid urotropine are added until a pH of 6 is reached.

In the case of the lead titration, $20.30\,\mathrm{mL}$ of EDTA solution ($c = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol/L}$) is required up to the equivalence point and a color change from blue to yellow. To determine the calcium ion concentration, the pH of the titrated solution is raised to 12 using $22.3\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a NaOH solution.

The solution turns blue again. A further $13.40\,\mathrm{mL}$ EDTA solution is added until the color of the indicator changes from blue to yellow again.

6.1 Calculate the concentrations of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ in the aqueous solution.

Having solved the analytical part of the problem, we now come to some equilibrium considerations. The following numerical values are given:

Acid dissociation constants of EDTA: $pK_{A1} = 2.00$; $pK_{A2} = 2.67$; $pK_{A3} = 6.16$; $pK_{A4} = 10.26$;

Stability constants of complexes: $\ce{[CaEDTA]^{2-}}$: $\log(K_\beta) = 10.70$; $\ce{[PbEDTA]^{2-}}$: $\log(K_\beta) = 18.04$;

Solubility products: $K_L(\ce{Ca(OH)2}) = 3.9\cdot10^{-6}$; $K_L(\ce{Pb(OH)2}) = 4.2\cdot10^{-15}$;

The stability constants of complexes refer to the complex formation with the completely protolysed form $\ce{EDTA^{4-}}$.

The total volume after the 1st titration is $127.8\,\mathrm{ml}$.

6.2 Calculate the concentration of free lead ions in the solution at the end of the first titration. Assume that in this calculation only the ions $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$, $\ce{EDTA^{4-}}$ and $\ce{[PbEDTA^{2-}]}$ must be considered. It is possibly necessary to make another assumption and to check if it is reasonable.

To determine the calcium ion concentration, the pH is raised to 12.0 as indicated above.

$\ce{Pb(OH)2}$ and/or $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$ could also precipitate.

6.3 Show by calculation that no precipitation occurs. For $[\ce{Pb^{2+}}]$, use the result of 6.2. If you were not able to get a result in 6.2, use $[\ce{Pb^{2+}}] = 3.0\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$. Use $[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]$ at the beginning of the 2nd titration.

An EDTA solution with a concentration of $0.0100\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ is used for the titration.

6.4 Calculate the concentrations of all EDTA species at pH = 6.00 without simplification. The autoprotolysis of water does not have to be considered, the activity coefficients of all ions are equal to 1.

problems.title: Fuel and Otto engine
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (7 points). Fuel and Otto engine

This task is about heptane (“hep") and iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethyl pentane, “oct“). Both are playing an important role in combustion engines. A few physico-chemical data are given all for a temperature of $298\,\mathrm{K}$. Due out this task in combustion reactions $\ce{H2O_{(g)}}$ should be formed.

heptane, liquid: $\rho = 0.680\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$; enthalpy of formation $\Delta_f H^\circ = -224.4\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

iso-octane, liquid: $\rho = 0.692\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$; enthalpy of combustion $\Delta_c H^\circ = -44328\,\mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}}$

further: $\Delta_f H^\circ(\ce{CO2}) = -393.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $\Delta_f H^\circ(\ce{H2O_{(g)}}) = -241.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

7.1 Indicate the molar masses:

hep: $\underline{\qquad\qquad}$ $\qquad$ oct: $\underline{\qquad\qquad}$

7.2 Calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion $\Delta_c H^\circ$ for heptane in the units given below.

$\underline{\qquad\qquad}$ kJ/mol $\qquad$ $\underline{\qquad\qquad}$ kJ/kg $\qquad$ $\underline{\qquad\qquad}$ kJ/L

7.3 Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation $\Delta_f H^\circ$ of iso-octane in kJ/mol.

Testing mixtures of n-heptane and iso-octane are of special importance. They are burnt in standardized test engines to get a measure for knock resistance for several fuels (engine knocking = ignitions in the motor cylinder at wrong time).

A fuel having the same knock resistance as an oct-hep-test mixture receives the volume fraction of octane of the latter as RON (“researched octane number"). Pure iso-octane has RON=100, pure heptane RON = 0.

Let us consider a test mixture with RON = 93, that means a volume fraction of 93% oct.

7.4 Calculate the density of this test mixture in g/L.

7.5 Calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion for the test mixture in kJ/mol.

7.6 Calculate the standard entropy and the standard Gibbs energy of mixing for $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the test mixture at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

The Otto engine, for which most of the fuels are being tested, is a heat engine. We will keep things simple and consider an idealized “thermodynamic" Otto-cycle using air as a working gas that shall behave ideal under all circumstances.

For air the molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_{V,m} = 20.85\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, the heat capacity ratio is $\gamma = 1{,}40$. We take all four steps as being reversible. The $pV$-diagram shows the circle:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2017-7-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{A } (1\to2) & \text{isentropic (adiabatic) compression} \\ \text{B } (2\to3) & \text{isochoric heating} \\ \text{C } (3\to4) & \text{isentropic (adiabatic) expansion (the power stroke of an Otto engine)} \\ \text{D } (4\to1) & \text{isochoric cooling} \end{array}$$

7.7 In which of the four steps (A-B-C-D) no work is done? Indicate the correct letter(s):

7.8 In one of the four steps (A-B-C-D) the combustion of the fuel takes place – so fast, that the Volume can be considered constant. Indicate the correct letter:

7.9 In one of the four steps (A-B-C-D) the entropy of the working gas is lowered. Indicate the correct letter:

For the four vertices in the $pV$-diagram the following data is known

$T_1 = 15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $p_1 = 100\,\mathrm{kPa}$; $\qquad T_3 = 1800\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$

The cylinder has a displacement of $1.00\,\mathrm{L}$. The displacement equals the difference $V_1 - V_2$. The dead volume $V_2$, is 15% of the maximum volume $V_1$.

7.10 Indicate $V_1$ and $V_2$.

7.11 Calculate $T_2$ and $T_4$.

7.12 Calculate the molar amount of air in the cylinder.

7.13 Calculate the changes in internal energy...

... for step A ($\Delta_\mathrm{A} U$)

... for step B ($\Delta_\mathrm{B} U$)

... for step C ($\Delta_\mathrm{C} U$)

... for step D ($\Delta_\mathrm{D} U$)

The efficiency $\eta$ is the ratio of heat added ($q$) to the total work $w$ done by the machine.

7.14 Calculate the efficiency of the idealized Otto engine.

problems.title: Determining the Concentration of Lead(II) in 1950
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (8 points). Determining the Concentration of Lead(II) in 1950

An interesting method to determine lead(II) ions in aqueous solutions was developed in the 1950s. It will be described in the following paragraphs:

$10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the sample to be analyzed for its content of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ions are transferred into a separatory funnel of a volume $V = 250\,\mathrm{mL}$. To this sample $75.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of cyanide solution described below are added to mask interfering cations:

Preparing the cyanide solution:

$3.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ potassium cyanide solution (10.0%, density $1.07\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) are added to $35.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ concentrated aqueous ammonia solution (35.0%, density $0.880\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$). Water is added to this mixture to reach a volume of $100\,\mathrm{mL}$.

The pH of the mixture in the separatory funnel is lowered to pH = 9.50 by adding hydrochloric acid ($6.00\,\mathrm{M}$). This is followed by adding $7.50\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a solution containing the complexing agent Dithizone in tetrachloromethane (0.00500 % (w/V), density $1.594\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) and $17.50\,\mathrm{mL}$ tetrachloromethane. During this step, Dithizone forms a coordination complex with the lead(II) ions that dissolves very well in tetrachloromethane. The mixture is agitated followed by waiting for phase separation. During this step the complex between lead and Dithizone transfers to the organic phase almost quantitatively. Finally, the absorbance of the organic phase is determined photometrically at a wavelength of $\lambda = 515\,\mathrm{nm}$. The molar extinction coefficient of the lead-Dithizone complex is $\varepsilon = 66450\,\mathrm{L\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot cm^{-1}}$.

The complexing agent Dithizone ($\ce{H2Dz}$) is a bidentate ligand and has the following structure:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2018-1-fig1.png

Equation for the coordination reaction:

$$\ce{2 H2Dz + Pb^{2+} <=> Pb(HDz)2 + 2 H+}$$

The extraction follows:

$$K_\mathrm{Ex} = \frac{[\ce{Pb(HDz)2}]_\mathrm{org}\cdot[\ce{H+}]^2}{[\ce{H2Dz}]_\mathrm{org}^2\cdot[\ce{Pb^{2+}}]} = 5.60$$

$$\begin{array}{l|c} & \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} \\ \hline \text{Hydrochloric acid} & -6.00 \\ \text{Ammonium ion} & 9.25 \\ \text{Hydrocyanic acid} & 9.40 \end{array}$$

1.1 Calculate the volume of hydrochloric acid necessary to reach pH=9.5. Neglect any possible influence of potassium cyanide and lead(II) ions for your calculation.

1.2 Give the pH value for which you expect substantial formation of hydrocyanic acid (i.e. at which the concentration of hydrocyanic acid exceeds that of cyanide ions) and under which the solution should not fall below.

1.3 Calculate the maximum concentration of lead in a sample (in mol/L) that can be analyzed with this method.

1.4 Calculate the lead concentration of a sample for an absorbance of $A = 0.328$ measured in a cuvette of $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ path length. Assume complete complexation and extraction.

At pH = 9.50 lead ions are present in different compounds determined by the following equilibria:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Pb^{2+} + H2O <=> PbOH+ + H+} & K_1 = \dfrac{[\ce{PbOH+}]\cdot[\ce{H+}]}{[\ce{Pb^{2+}}]} = 3.00\cdot10^{-7} \\[2ex] \ce{Pb^{2+} + 2 H2O <=> Pb(OH)2 + 2 H+} & K_2 = \dfrac{[\ce{Pb(OH)2}]\cdot[\ce{H+}]^2}{[\ce{Pb^{2+}}]} = 3.00\cdot10^{-18} \\[2ex] \ce{Pb^{2+} + 2 H2O <=> HPbO2- + 3 H+} & K_3 = \dfrac{[\ce{HPbO2-}]\cdot[\ce{H+}]^3}{[\ce{Pb^{2+}}]} = 7.00\cdot10^{-29} \end{array}$$

1.5 Calculate the percentual amounts of the different lead-containing species at pH=9.5.

Base the next calculation on the following conditions: If you did not obtain a result in 1.1, assume that $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ of hydrochloric acid were added. Furthermore, assume that the extraction step does not change pH of the aqueous solution. Also, neglect the two lead-contining species $\ce{Pb(OH)2}$ and $\ce{HPbO2-}$. If you make further assumputions for your calculation, you need to show with your result that they were correct and valid (error < 1%).

1.6 Calculate the total concentration of all lead species in the aqueous phase after extracting with the abovementioned amount of dithizone in tetrachloromethane. Base your calculation on a sample that initially contained $c = 1.00\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ Pb(II).

problems.problem:
Problem 2 (8 points). Chromium and its Compounds: Electrochemistry & Kinetics

A. Galvanic production of Chromium

Chromium metal coatings can be produced by electrolysis in aqueous solutions of chromic acid ($\ce{H2CrO4}$).

Electrolysis was carried out for 7.00 hours at a current of $1500\,\mathrm{A}$. No changes occurred on the inert anode. At the cathode, hydrogen developed as as side product thus reducing the current yield for the deposition of chromium. At standard conditions ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$) this resulted in the formation of $4.15\,\mathrm{m^3}$ hydrogen. Gas also developed on the anode.

2.1 Give balanced equations for all electrode processes.

• Cathode:
• Anode:

2.2 Calculate the current yield for the deposition of chromium on the cathode.

2.3 Calculate the mass of chromium deposited.

2.4 Calculate the volume of the gas having developed on the anode at standard conditions ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$).

B. Electrochemistry of Chromium and its Compounds

Chromium (from Greek χρωμα = color) received its name from that fact that its compounds and ions show many different colors.

Below, you find an incomplete Latimer diagram for some of these coloured ions at pH = 0. All potentials are given in Volt.

$$\underset{\text{orange}}{\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}} \xrightarrow{\ +0.55\ } \underset{\text{red}}{\text{Cr(V)}} \xrightarrow{\ +1.34\ } \underset{\text{green}}{\text{Cr(IV)}} \xrightarrow{\quad x\quad} \underset{\text{purple}}{\ce{Cr^{3+}}} \xrightarrow{\ -0.424\ } \underset{\text{blue}}{\ce{Cr^{2+}}} \xrightarrow{\quad y\quad} \text{Cr}$$

[In the printed diagram, a further arrow labelled +0.295 leads above the chain from $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ to Cr, and an arrow labelled −0.741 leads below the chain from $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ to Cr.]

2.5 Calculate the missing potentials $x$ and $y$.

2.6 Demonstrate that Cr(IV) can disproportionate to Cr(III) and Cr(VI) via suitable calculation.

2.7 Calculate the equilibrium constant for this disproportioning reaction at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

2.8 Does Cr(II) tend to disproportionate to Cr(III) and Cr(0)? Tick the correct box and give a reason for your choice based on the Frost diagram of the relevant species.

• yes, tends to disproportionate
• no, does not tend to disproportionate

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2018-2-fig1.png

The so-called Pourbaix diagram (see right) results from plotting the redox potentials of all chromium species against pH. It is based on the condition that the activities of all species participating in any equilibrium are $a = 1$, except for $\ce{H+}$ ($\ce{H3O+}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2018-2-fig2.png

2.9 Name two species showing pH-independent redox reaction in the diagram, at least within a certain pH-range.

2.10 Name two species showing protolysis that does not depend on pontential.

Analytical Chemistry often uses the redox system dichromate/chromium(III). Its standard potential is $E^\circ(\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}|\ce{Cr^{3+}}) = +1.33\,\mathrm{V}$.

2.11 In which pH range does $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ react to $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$?

2.12 Formulate the half equation for the redox pair $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}|\ce{Cr^{3+}}$.

2.13 Derive an equation $E = f(\mathrm{pH})$ for the line between the two species $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ and $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. (Assumption: the activities of the chromium species do not change).

2.14 Use this derived linear function to calculate $E$ at pH=2.

C. Kinetics – Chromium and Ethanol

Oxidizing $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$ with Chromium(VI) formerly was the basis to determine the ethanol content in breath ("chemical alco test"). The reaction can also be used in analysis. Diluted $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ solutions in strongly acidic solution (in this case 3.6 M HCl) yield $\ce{HCrO4-}$ ions, the oxidizing compound during the reaction.

2.15 Formulate a balanced equation for the reaction of $\ce{HCrO4-}$ with ethanol to $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ und ethanoic acid.

At the given conditions the rate law for the overall reaction is:

$$v = -\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{HCrO4-}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k\cdot[\ce{HCrO4-}]^x$$

with reaction order $x$ being an integer. After waiting for different reaction times $t$, $[\ce{HCrO4-}]_t$ was determined by iodometric titration. Iodine reacted with thiosulfate ($c = 0.020\,\mathrm{mol/L}$) following $\ce{2 S2O3^{2-} + I2 <=> 2 I- + S4O6^{2-}}$. As usual, the end point was marked by adding starch. Iodine previously had been formed by reaction of remaining $\ce{HCrO4-}$ with iodide. Hence it was possible to calculate $[\ce{HCrO4-}]_t$ from the amount of thiosulfate solution used during titration.

For each analysis a sample volume of $10.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ was used. This led to the following values:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Reaction time } t\ /\ \mathrm{min} & 0 & 10 & 20 & 30 & 40 \\ \hline \text{Titration volume } V(\ce{S2O3^{2-}})\ /\ \mathrm{mL} & \text{---} & 11.7 & 9.10 & 7.15 & 5.60 \\ \hline [\ce{HCrO4-}]_t\ /\ \mathrm{mol/L} & 0.0100 & 0.0078 & 0.0061 & 0.0048 & 0.0037 \\ \hline \ln[\ce{HCrO4-}]_t & -4.61 & -4.85 & -5.10 & -5.35 & -5.59 \\ \hline \dfrac{1}{[\ce{HCrO4-}]_t} & 100 & 128 & 165 & 210 & 268 \end{array}$$

2.16 As an example, calculate the concentration $[\ce{HCrO4-}]_t$ for a titration volume $V(\ce{S2O3^{2-}}) = 10.3\,\mathrm{mL}$.

2.17 Determine the reaction order $x$, by plotting concentration vs time in a suitable graph. Choose reasonable dimensions on each axis.

2.18 Calculate the rate constant $k$ and give the result with correct units.

Problem 3 (17 points). Organic Syntheses

A. Polymerization

Polylactides, short PLA, are polymerized through so-called ring opening polymerization (ROP). They were first described in 1845 by Théophile-Jules Pelouze, who observed that oligomers and polymers form during the isolation of lactic acid. PLA-based thermoplasts gain increasing popularity because they are biodegradable. For instance, they compete with standard PE foils as mulch films in agriculture and gardening. A process leading to PLA from lactides was developed in 1932 and patented in 1954 by DuPont, a large chemical company.

Mark the repetitive unit in the product (after step 3) in the usual way.

B. Synthesis of a caffeic acid derivative

How is this name reaction called?

C. Woodward synthesis of Colchicine

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2018-3-fig3.png

Colchicine is the main alkaloid of the autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale). It is one of the most prominent natural products. First attempts of total synthesis in the 1950s set milestones for the synthesis of natural products. Only very few target compounds have been synthesized in such multifaceted ways as colchicine. The special feature of this synthesis was that it strategically introduces the nitrogen functionality at C-7 at a very early stage of the protocol. problems.problem:
Problem 4 (17 points). Nitrogen and its Compounds

This problem deals with Nitrogen and some of its compounds. It elucidates aspects of chemical properties and molecular structure as well as thermodynamic and kinetic aspects.

A. The Nitrogen Molecule – a Comparison

In contrast to molecular oxygen molecular nitrogen is rather inert. Comparing the corresponding MO schemes can explain this inertness. The following figure shows MO schemes of $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{O2}$, and $\ce{NH3}$, one of the most important nitrogen compounds, respectively.

B. Ammonia

Every year some 180 million metric tons of ammonia are produced, which makes it one of the most important commodity chemicals. Almost all ammonia is synthesized through the Haber-Bosch process based on the following reaction:

$$\ce{N2}_\mathrm{(g)} + \ce{3 H2}_\mathrm{(g)} \ce{->} \ce{2 NH3}_\mathrm{(g)} \qquad \text{(R 4.1)}$$

Find some thermodynamic data at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ you will need during the following calculations:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ\ /\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} & S^\circ\ /\ \mathrm{J/molK} & C_p^\circ\ /\ \mathrm{J/molK} \\ \hline \ce{N2}_\mathrm{(g)} & 0 & 191.6 & 29.1 \\ \ce{H2}_\mathrm{(g)} & 0 & 130.7 & 28.8 \\ \ce{NH3}_\mathrm{(g)} & -45.9 & 192.8 & \end{array}$$

This gigantic weapon will produce the abovementioned 180 million metric tons of ammonia in a gigantic bomb calorimeter to be used later for destroying the assigned planetary target.

4.4 Calculate the overall quantity of heat $Q_2$ released for one batch of ammonia in the bomb calorimeter at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

4.5 Calculate the sum mass of educts the death star needs to hold for one load of ammonia.

Let us now return to science without fiction. The Haber Bosch process is often discussed when introducing chemical equilibrium.

4.6 Calculate $K_p$ for the formation of ammonia following equation R 4.1 at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

Ammonia synthesis often takes place at $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to achieve higher reaction rate.

C. Bond breaking in Nitrogen and Kinetic Isotope Effect

One limitation of ammonia synthesis lies in the fact that the activation energy of the uncatalyzed reaction is extraordinarily high. One can estimate its value from the reaction enthalpy of the dissociation of $\ce{N2}$ and $\ce{H2}$ in the gas phase:

$$\ce{1/2 N2 + 3/2 H2 -> N + 3 H} \qquad \Delta_\mathrm{R}H = E_\mathrm{A}$$

The following enthalpies are given:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{N + H -> NH} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H = -314\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \ce{NH + H -> NH2} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H = -389\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \ce{NH2 + H -> NH3} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H = -460\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \text{Mass in amu} & \text{Frequency of occurrence} \\ \hline \ce{^{14}N} & 14.0031 & 99.634\,\% \\ \ce{^{15}N} & 15.0001 & 0.366\,\% \end{array}$$

D. Catalysis

Since its earliest days, ammonia synthesis is based on an iron-based catalyst found by Alwin Mittasch as the result of tedious chemical legwork. It took until the 1980s that Gerhard Ertl (Nobel Prize for Chemistry 2007) elucidated in detail how this catalyst works. The individual steps during heterogeneous catalysis are complex. E. Ultrafast Reaction of Ammonia in Aqueous Solution

The following equilibrium is always reached very fast:

F. Further Compounds containing N and H

In addition to ammonia, other compounds containing N and H exist. For instance, you may already have heard of hydrazine, which is used as rocket fuel. The chemical element chromium comprises different nuclides ranging from mass number 41 to 68. $\ce{^{50}Cr}$, $\ce{^{52}Cr}$, $\ce{^{53}Cr}$, and $\ce{^{54}Cr}$ are stable isotopes. The unstable isotope $\ce{^{51}Cr}$ is applied intravenously, for instance to determine the volumes and masses of red blood cells. $\ce{^{51}Cr}$ disintegrates through electron capture. B. Chromium in Complexes and Ionic Lattices

Then an excess of silver nitrate solution was added. The resulting precipitate was filtered, washed, dried, and weighed: $m_\mathrm{precipitate} = 0.287\,\mathrm{g}$.

Many compounds of type $\ce{AB2O4}$ crystallize in the so-called spinel-type crystal structure.

In normal spinels, $\ce{O^{2-}}$-ions form a cubic face-centered structure. One eigth of the tetrahedral voids is occupied by – mostly bivalent – A-ions. Half the octahedral voids are occupied by – mostly trivalent – B-ions.

Inverse spinels also consist of compounds $\ce{AB2O4}$ and the same crystal lattice. However, the A-ions in this case occupy one quarter of the octahedral voids, the B-ions one quarter of the octahedral and one eighth of the tetrahedral voids. Hence again one half of the octahedral voids and one eighth of the tetrahedral voids are occupied..

One can predict if a spinel is normal or inverse by comparing the ligand field stabilization energies LSFE of the two species. For $\ce{FeCr2O4}$, a spinel, there are two possibilities: Normal spinel $\mathrm{Fe^{T}Cr^{O}Cr^{O}O_4}$, and inverse spinel $\mathrm{Fe^{O}Cr^{T}Cr^{O}O_4}$; here, $^\mathrm{O}$ and $^\mathrm{T}$ denote octahedral and tetrahedral voids, respectively. $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ comprises 6 d electrons, $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ 3 d electrons. In all cases high spin complexes are preferred over low-spin complexes.

Problem 3 (4 points). Electrochemistry: Copper and Other Metals

A. Composition of a 10-cent coin.

Coins of denominations 10, 20, and 50 cents consist of so-called Nordic Gold, an alloy of copper, zinc, aluminum, and tin. The aim of this problem is to determine the composition of this alloy in % (m/m).

In a first step, a 10-cent-coin weighing $4.100\,\mathrm{g}$ is dissolved in diluted hydrochloric acid. This generates $363.9\,\mathrm{mL}$ Hydrogen (Pressure $p = 1.013\,\mathrm{bar}$; $298\,\mathrm{K}$).

The undissolved residue (a reddish metal) is completely dissolved in concentrated nitric acid and then electrolyzed after appropriate pre-treatment.

Completely depositing it on the cathode requires 16.71 minutes at a current of $I = 13\,\mathrm{A}$ and 85% current efficiency.

$N$-Benzoyl-$N$-phenylhydroxylamine ($\ce{C6H5CON(OH)C6H5}$) precipitates tin dissolved in the hydrochloric acid and yields the complex $\ce{(C13H11O2N)2SnCl2}$. This results in $0.213\,\mathrm{g}$ of the complex ($M = 616.11\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$).

Problem 4 (10 points). Energy and Conjugated Systems

A. Propene

Propene is regarded one of the most important raw materials for organic secondary products. The estimated annual world production is more than 50 million (metric) tons. There are several ways to produce propene. Olefin metathesis is one possible way:

$$\ce{CH2=CH2_{(g)} + CH3-CH=CH-CH3_{(g)} -> 2 H2C=CH-CH3_{(g)}}$$

Find some thermodynamic data at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ for your further calculations:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ\ /\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & \Delta_\mathrm{c}H^\circ\ /\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & S^\circ\ /\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} & C_p^\circ\ /\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{Ethene}_{(g)} & 52.4 & & 219.3 & 42.9 \\ \text{But-2-ene}_{(g)} & -7.7 & & 301.0 & 80.2 \\ \text{Propene}_{(g)} & 20.4 & -2058.0 & 266.8 & 64.3 \\ \text{Propane}_{(g)} & & -2220.0 & & \\ \ce{H2}_{(g)} & & -286.5 & & \end{array}$$

4.1 Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$, $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^\circ$, and $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ$, as well as $K_p$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

In reality, the reaction takes place at higher temperatures, such as $436\,\mathrm{K}$.

4.2 Calculate the heat that is set free at isobaric conditions when producing $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ Propene at $436\,\mathrm{K}$.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of Propane is another way to produce Propene:

$$\ce{C3H8_{(g)} -> C3H6_{(g)} + H2_{(g)}}$$

4.3 Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{r}U^\circ$ for for this reaction at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

B. Propene in Action – the Allyl System

Reactions involving propene often give rise to reactive species, which are also interesting from the point of theory of chemical binding. They are: The allyl cation, the allyl anion, and the allyl radical:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2019-4-fig1.png

These three species share a common, planar carbon backbone as well as the same $\pi$ molecular orbitals. Those can be calculated with the Hückel approximation.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \varphi_1 = 0.500\chi_1 + 0.707\chi_2 + 0.500\chi_3 & E_1 = \alpha + 1.414\beta \\ \varphi_2 = 0.707\chi_1 - 0.707\chi_3 & E_2 = \,? \\ \varphi_3 = 0.500\chi_1 - 0.707\chi_2 + 0.500\chi_3 & E_3 = \alpha - 1.414\beta \end{array}$$

$E_2 =$ ________

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2019-4-fig3.png

The charges at the C atoms and the bond orders can be calculated using the expressions of the molecular orbitals:

$$q_j = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{occ} n_i\, c_{ij}^2 \qquad\qquad I_{rs} = \sum_{i=1}^{occ} n_i\, c_{ir}\, c_{is}$$

C. Hexatriene

The Latin word conjugare means to connect, make friends, marry – and apparently $\pi$-electrons like to do that. Hexatriene is an acyclic system that easily allows one to study the conjugation of $\pi$-molecular orbitals (MO) following the Hückel approximation:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2019-4-fig4.png

problems.title: Tartar Equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (7 points). Tartar Equilibrium

Several hundred compounds can be determined in wine. Organic acids represent an important group of those. L-(+) tartaric acid, L-(-) malic acid, and citric acid are the most important organic acids in wine.

L-(+)-tartaric acid ((2R,3R)-2,3-Dihydroxybutane diacid) is a diprotic acid with $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A}$-values 2.98 and 4.34.

"Tartar" describes salts of tartaric acid that precipitate from wine – sometimes after storing it for extended periods of time. Potassium hydrogentartrate and calcium tartrate are the most common of these salts. These two salts often form supersaturated solutions in wine, so that they crystallize long after bottling the wine.

White wine of the variety „Grüngipfler" at $17\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ contains a maximum concentration of $c^\mathrm{max} = 2.50\,\mathrm{g}$ potassium hydrogentartrate in 1 L wine.

5.1 Give the empirical formula and the molar mass of potassium hydrogentartrate.

5.2 Calculate the solubility product of this salt at those conditions.

To partially remove tartar, this wine is cooled to $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ prior to bottling. This decreases the solubility of potassium hydrogentartrate to $1.13\,\mathrm{g/L}$. The insoluble fraction precipitates and is removed. Then, the wine is re-heated to $17\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

5.3 Calculate the molar concentration of potassium hydrogentartrate in this wine. For your calculation assume that the density of wine remains constantly at $1000\,\mathrm{g/L}$ despite changing temperature.

Adding potassium hydrogencarbonate is a frequent technique to de-acidify wine.

5.4 How much – i.e. which mass – potassium hydrogencarbonate could one add to the wine in Problem 5.3 per liter after partially removing potassium hydrogentartrate, before one could expect that solid potassium hydrogentartrate forms anew. To simplify the problem, assume that adding potassium hydrogencarbonate to the wine does not substantially change the pH of wine and that hence the molar concentration of hydrogentartrate ions does not change either. Use the solubility product calculated in Problem 5.2. If you did not achieve a result there, use the value $K_{SP}^{17^\circ} = 0.0002$.

White wine of the variety „Grüngipfler" is saturated in potassium hydrogentartrate at a temperature of $T = 17\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at pH = 3.10. Saturation concentration is $2.50\,\mathrm{g/L}$.

5.5 Calculate the sum of concentrations of all tartaric acid species in this wine.

One adds $1500\,\mathrm{mg/L}$ Potassium hydrogen carbonate to the wine from Problem 5.5 to de-acidify it. This increases the pH to pH = 3.45.

5.6 Calculate the concentrations of all tartaric acid species at this pH without considering precipitation reactions. In case you did not get a result for the total concentration of all tartaric acid species in Problem 5.5, use $c_{tot} = 0.03\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ for your calculations.

5.7 Now, calculate the mass of solid potassium hydrogen tartrate precipitating after adding potassium hydrogencarbonate in Problem 5.6. For the sake of simplicity, assume that no hydrogentartrate is formed or consumed from other tartaric acid species during this process. Furthermore, assume that all potassium that was initially present in the wine originates from potassium hydrogentartrate.

Use the solubility product calculated in Problem 5.2. If you did not achieve a result there, use the value $K_{SP}^{17^\circ} = 0.0002$.

problems.problem:
Problem 6 (5 points). Kinetics

A. Reaction iodate - iodide

The following reaction is useful for analyzing the concentration of Iodide ions:

$$\ce{IO3^-(aq) + 5 I^-(aq) + 6 H+ -> 3 I2(aq) + 3 H2O(l)}$$

Assessing the reaction rate of this reaction at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ yields the following results:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & [\ce{I-}],\ \mathrm{M} & [\ce{IO3-}],\ \mathrm{M} & [\ce{H+}],\ \mathrm{M} & \text{Reaction rate, }\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}\cdot s^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & 0.010 & 0.10 & 0.010 & 0.60 \\ 2 & 0.040 & 0.10 & 0.010 & 2.40 \\ 3 & 0.010 & 0.30 & 0.010 & 5.40 \\ 4 & 0.010 & 0.10 & 0.020 & 2.40 \end{array}$$

6.1 Determine the order of the reaction regarding the three species. Demonstrate your line of thoughts.

i) Regarding $\ce{I-}$

ii) Regarding $\ce{IO3-}$

iii) Regarding $\ce{H+}$

6.2 Specify the rate law and calculate the rate constant $k$.

6.3 The activation energy of the reaction above at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $E_\mathrm{A} = 84\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$. Calculate by which factor the reaction rate increases, if one decreases the activation energy (e.g. with a catalyst) by $10\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

B. Michaelis-Menten Kinetics

In some cases, one can assume a steady state to approximate investigations of kinetics. There is one prerequisite to this, namely that the concentrations of all intermediate products are constant during most of the time during the reaction.

This approach is especially feasible for biochemical reactions of the following type:

$$\ce{S + E <=>[k_a][k_{-a}] ES ->[k_b] P + E}$$

S = Substrate (e.g. Penicillin); E = Enzyme (e.g. $\beta$-Lactamase); ES = Enzyme-Substrate complex; P = Product.

$[\mathrm{E}]_{tot}$ = Total concentration of E ($[\mathrm{E}] + [\mathrm{ES}]$)

One assumes that the preceding equilibrium is reached very rapidly, that the reverse reaction of P into ES can be neglected, and that [S] is much larger than [E].

6.4 Show that these assumptions allow you to derive the expression $[\mathrm{ES}] = \dfrac{[\mathrm{E}]_{tot}\cdot[\mathrm{S}]}{K_M + [\mathrm{S}]}$, where the Michaelis-Menten constant is $K_M = \dfrac{k_{-a} + k_b}{k_a}$.

6.5 Show that the maximum reaction rate is $\left(\dfrac{d[\mathrm{P}]}{dt}\right)_{max} = v_{max} = k_b\cdot[\mathrm{E}]_{tot}$.

6.6 Derive the Michaelis-Menten equation $v = \dfrac{v_{max}\cdot[\mathrm{S}]}{K_M + [\mathrm{S}]}$ from 6.4 and 6.5.

6.7 Read the value for $K_M$ from the curve below showing $v = f([\mathrm{S}])$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2019-6-fig1.png

Often the relationship between $v$ and $[\mathrm{S}]$ is shown in a so called Lineweaver-Burk-Plot $\dfrac{1}{v} = f\left(\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{S}]}\right)$.

6.8 Show that $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{K_M}{v_{max}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{S}]} + \dfrac{1}{v_{max}}$.

The table below shows the initial reaction rates depending on substrate concentration at an enzyme concentration of $E_{tot} = 1.0\cdot10^{-9}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} [\mathrm{S}]_0\cdot10^{-6}\text{ in }\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}} & 3.0 & 5.0 & 10 & 20 \\ \hline v_0\cdot10^{-5}\text{ in }\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}} & 1.06 & 1.55 & 2.37 & 3.21 \end{array}$$

6.9 Determine the Michaelis constant $K_M$ and the rate constant $k_b$ from the Lineweaver-Burk-plot.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2019-6-fig2.png

A different enzyme reaction yielded a Michaelis constant of $K_M = 1.5\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$. The initial substrate concentration is $[\mathrm{S}] = 3\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$.

6.10 Calculate the fraction of enzyme molecules ($f_{ES}$) that bind substrate.

problems.title: Evaporating and Cooling
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (6 points). Evaporating and Cooling

The enthalpy of vaporization of a solvent depends on the concentration of compounds dissolved in it. It is not always simple to measure it. The Bubble Column Evaporator is an interesting method for that purpose. It can also serve as a didactic experiment in studies (J. Chem. Educ. 2016, 93, 1642-1646).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2019-7-fig1.png

In the experiment dry gas bubbles (1-3 mm diameter) rise from the bottom of the column through a salt solution. Within a few tenths of a second, the interior of the bubbles is saturated with water vapor. This evaporation process withdraws heat from the water. Hence the temperature at the top ($T_\mathrm{o}$) of the experimental setup is lower, than at the bottom ($T_\mathrm{u}$). After some time, the system reaches steady state, at which both temperatures do not change any more. Hence the heat delivered via the dry bubbles exclusively evaporates water. This does not withdraw heat from the solution. One can hence balance the energy loss as follows:

$$V\cdot(c_p\,\Delta T + \Delta p) = V\cdot\rho_V\cdot\Delta_{vap}H$$

Energy loss of the bubbles = Enthalpy of vaporization

Here, $\Delta T = T_\mathrm{u} - T_\mathrm{o}$ means the difference in temperature between bottom and top end, , $c_p$ the specific heat capacity of the gas (in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$); $\Delta p$ is the difference in pressure between the gas flowing into the system and the gas leaving the solution at atmospheric pressure; $\rho_V$ is the the density of water vapor. Dividing this equation by $V$ yields Energy per Volume.

Below find the data for an experiment carried out with 0.5M NaCl solution:

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Inlet temperature } T_\mathrm{u} & 54.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \text{Outlet temperature } T_\mathrm{o} & 21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \text{Heat capacity of the gas used } c_p & 1204\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}} \\ \text{Water vapor density } \rho_V \text{ (at } T_\mathrm{o}\text{)} & 1.030\,\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}} \\ \text{Inlet pressure } p_\mathrm{u} & 105453\,\mathrm{Pa} \\ \text{Outlet pressure (atmospheric pressure) } p_\mathrm{o} & 101325\,\mathrm{Pa} \\ \text{Gas flow rate} & 0.18\,\mathrm{L\,s^{-1}} \end{array}$$

Further data:

$$\begin{array}{l|l} c_p\text{(air)} & 1.008\,\mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ c_p(\ce{N2}) & 1.040\,\mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \end{array}$$

To simplify, one can assume that air consists of 21.0% Oxygen and 79.0% Nitrogen.

To get an impression of heat quantities, let us begin with a little story from winter: someone left the windows of lecture hall "Scientia" (Latin for "Science"; the room where this test takes place) open overnight. Temperature dropped to $-5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

7.1 Calculate the energy necessary to reheat the air in the room to $22\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (at atmospheric pressure).

Let us switch back to the bubble experiment according to the figure above.

7.2 Calculate the number of gas bubbles occurring per second, assuming a mean bubble diameter of 2mm.

7.3 Tick the correct boxes

When rising through the column, pressure in the gas

• increases
• decreases

• Work is performed on the bubbles.
• The bubbles perform work.

This work needs to be

• added
• subtracted

to/from the heat transferred by the gas to calculate the Enthalpy of Vaporization.

7.4 Calculate the Enthalpy of Vaporization $\Delta_{vap}H$ determined during the experiment above.

7.5 Use calculation to decide if air or nitrogen had been used for the experiment.

7.6 Calculate the vapor pressure of water above the salt solution from the vapor density at temperature $T_\mathrm{o}$.

The Enthalpy of Vaporization of pure water at $16\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is: $2463.0\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, its vapor pressure at this temperature is: $1.8188\,\mathrm{kPa}$

7.7 Calculate the vapor pressure of pure water at $T_\mathrm{o}$ and tick the correct boxes.

• The vapor pressure of water decreases by adding salt.
• The vapor pressure of water increases by adding salt.

There were considerations to utilize such a setup on a larger scale for evaporation cooling. For this purpose, an experiment took place using a gas flow rate of $150\,\mathrm{m^3/h}$. All other parameters (temperatures, pressures, …) remained constant.

7.8 Calculate the cooling power of the setup at this flow rate, i.e. at $150\,\mathrm{m^3/h}$.

The air blower used takes in air at atmospheric pressure and generates $262\,\mathrm{mbar}$ overpressure. It uses an electric motor that takes up $2.2\,\mathrm{kW}$ power. The fraction of power not used for compressing the gas leaves the mechanism in the form of heat.

7.9 Calculate the mechanical power of the air blower.

problems.title: Isomer counting by Alfred Werner and complexes of cobalt
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (6 points). Isomer counting by Alfred Werner and complexes of cobalt

Author: N. Langer

Alfred Werner used the technique of isomer counting to deduce the structure of metal complexes with coordination number of six. Three of the shapes he considered are shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-1-fig1.png

In each structure, the empty circle shows the location of the central metal atom and the filled circles show the location of the ligands. Structure $\mathbf{X}$ is hexagonal planar, structure $\mathbf{Y}$ is trigonal prismatic and structure $\mathbf{Z}$ is octahedral.

For each of the three shapes, there is just one structure when all of the ligands are the same, i.e. when the complex has the general formula $\ce{MA6}$ where A is the ligand. However, when achiral ligands A are substituted by one or more achiral ligands, it may be possible for each structure to form geometrical isomers. It might also be possible for one or more of the geometrical isomers to be optically active and exist as pairs of enantiomers.

The monodentate ligands A are substituted by monodentate ligands B or by symmetrical bidentate ligands, denoted C-C. Bidentate ligand C-C can only link between two atoms on adjacent positions, i.e. those positions connected by a line in the structures $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$.

1.1 In the answer sheet, create the table below. Indicate how many geometric isomers exist for each of the three structures $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$. Write the number of possible geometric isomers in each box. If one of the isomers occurs as a pair of enantiomers, add an asterisk * to the number.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{hexagonal planar } \mathbf{X} & \text{trigonal prismatic } \mathbf{Y} & \text{oktahedral } \mathbf{Z} \\ \hline \ce{MA6} & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \ce{MA4B2} & & & \\ \ce{MA4(C-C)} & & & \\ \ce{MA2(C-C)2} & & & \end{array}$$

[The three right-hand columns are headed "number of predicted geometric isomers".]

There are no known complexes that adopt the hexagonal planar geometry $\mathbf{X}$, but structures are known for both the trigonal prismatic geometry $\mathbf{Y}$ and the octahedral geometry $\mathbf{Z}$. In these complexes, the orbitals derived from the metal d-orbitals have different energies depending on the geometry of the complex. The splitting patterns for the trigonal prismatic geometry and for the octahedral geometry are shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-1-fig2.png

1.2 Draw the energy level diagram for both coordinations/shapes and label which d-orbitals are which.

The complexes $\ce{[Mn(H2O)6]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^{2-}}$ are both octahedral. One has a magnetic moment of $5{,}9\,\mu_\mathrm{B}$, the other has a magnetic moment of $3{,}9\,\mu_\mathrm{B}$.

1.3 Draw an occupancy scheme for the d-orbitals for both complexes and write the appropriate magnetic moment.

Octahedral complexes are far more common than trigonal prismatic. Werner isolated five compounds $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$ containing Co(III), Cl, and $\ce{NH3}$ only, each of which contained one octahedral complex. Werner's five compounds had the molar conductivities shown below. The conductivities are extrapolated to infinite dilution and are expressed in arbitrary units. Compound G does not react with aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$; compounds $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$ react with different stoichiometric ratios of aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$; $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ react with the same stoichiometric ratio of aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \mathbf{C} & \mathbf{D} & \mathbf{E} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{G} \\ \hline \text{Molar conductivity in }\mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}} & 510 & 372 & 249 & 249 & \sim 0 \end{array}$$

1.5 Enter the IUPAC name, including the stereo descriptor of the cobalt(III) complex.

Many complexes exist as isomers, with a distinction being made between stereo and structural isomers.

1.6 Give the formula for an ionization isomer of $\ce{[Co(NH3)5(NO3)]SO4}$.

Cobalt(III) complexes are octahedral and intensely colored. Three complex compounds with ligand field splitting are listed in the table. The possible colors are yellow, orange-yellow, blue, and dark green.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \text{Complex} & \text{Ligand field splitting in }\mathrm{cm^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \ce{[Co(C2O4)6]^{3-}} & 18000 \\ \text{(ii)} & \ce{[Co(H2O)6]^{3+}} & 18200 \\ \text{(iii)} & \ce{[Co(NH3)6]^{3+}} & 22900 \\ \text{(iv)} & \ce{[Co(en)3]^{3-}} & 33500 \end{array}$$

1.7 Assign the correct color to each complex (e.g., write (vii) green).

Cobalt does not form only complex compounds. The olive green cobalt(II) oxide is formed from the elements at $1100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The ionic radius of $\ce{Co^{2+}}$ is $0{,}82\,\text{Å}$ and that of the oxide ion is $140\,\mathrm{pm}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-1-fig4.png

A and B are two different metal ions with different oxidation numbers that coordinate tetrahedrally and octahedrally with $\ce{O^{2-}}$ ions. In fact, tetrahedrally coordinated sites are often called A sites, and octahedrally coordinated sites are called B sites. The figure on the left introduces the unit cell of spinel. The right one shows the inner workings of the 8 cube parts, so to speak, and thus indicates exactly where which atoms are located. Cobalt compounds are used in medicine to treat cyanide poisoning. The person poisoned with cyanide receives an infusion with a solution of a chelate complex consisting of cobalt(II) and the hexavalent ligand $\ce{(EDTA)^{4-}}$. problems.title: Chlorine in the pool and equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (6 points). Chlorine in the pool and equilibrium

Author: W. Faber

Inexpensive frame pools are being sold more and more frequently in Austria. Such a frame pool was purchased to offer the teachers a balance to their hard work. This pool has a capacity of $17{,}00\,\mathrm{m^3}$. It was completely filled up with tap water and now has a temperature of $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. For further calculations, it can be assumed that the tap water initially contained no dissolved salts.

Then $50{,}00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of NaCl were added to the water in the pool and dissolved. A so-called "salt plant" is responsible for the disinfection of the pool water. Here the pool water is subjected to electrolysis, using a current of $3{,}79\,\mathrm{A}$. Chlorine gas is produced at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode.

2.1 Calculate the concentration of chloride ions in the pool water before the electrolysis.

2.2 Write the reaction equations for the cathodic and anodic processes.

2.3 Calculate the mass of chlorine gas produced per hour, assuming a complete electric yield.

2.4 Calculate the pH value of the pool if electrolysis was conducted for 10 hours and assuming that only the hydroxide ions formed at the cathode influence this pH value.

For further calculations, assume that in the pool mentioned above with a volume of $17{,}00\,\mathrm{m^3}$ after the addition of $50{,}00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of NaCl and several days of electrolysis, a total of $60{,}0\,\mathrm{g}$ of chlorine gas has dissolved in the water of the pool and that the pool contents has a stable pH of 9,50 and that none of the reactions taking place have a significant influence on the concentration of dissolved chloride ions or the pH value. The chlorine gas reacts with water according to the following equation:

$$\ce{Cl2_{(aq)} + 2 H2O <=> HOCl + H3O+ + Cl-} \qquad K = 4{,}20\cdot10^{-4}$$

As is common practice with reaction constants, the concentration of water is set to 1 for this constant. The hypochlorous acid HOCl formed is a weak acid with a $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ value of 7,54.

2.5 To determine which chlorine-containing oxidant plays the most significant role in preventing contamination of the pool, calculate the concentrations of dissolved chlorine gas, hypochlorous acid, and hypochlorite anion in equilibrium under the given conditions.

In the previous example, it was assumed that the pH value does not change during the reactions taking place. The actual change should now be determined. For simplification, we now assume that the entire $60{,}0\,\mathrm{g}$ chlorine gas is first converted into hypochlorous acid. The pH value before the introduction of the chlorine gas is again 9,50.

2.6 Calculate the pH value in the pool by taking into account the $\ce{H3O+}$ ions formed during the hydrolysis of the chlorine gas. Neglect the acid effect of the (weak) hypochlorous acid.

problems.title: Kinetics of air pollution
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (5 points). Kinetics of air pollution

Author: C. Hurban

A. Formation of NO

The one-step reaction, according to the following equation, plays a major role in the field of air pollution:

$$\ce{2 NO2(g) -> 2 NO(g) + O2(g)}$$

4.1 Express the reaction rate with respect to partial pressures of all three species.

In the left figure, the partial pressures of three species are plotted against time; the right figure shows a curve for the starting material.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-4-fig1.png

4.2 Which of the three curves on the left shows the temporal course of the oxygen partial pressure?

4.3 Specify the reaction order.

4.4 Specify the differential and integral rate law.

4.5 Derive an expression for the half-life $\tau$ from 4.4.

If $\ce{NO2}$ is filled into a container of $2{,}0\,\mathrm{L}$ with an initial pressure of $0{,}80\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 50% of the $\ce{NO2}$ is converted after 3,0 minutes.

4.6 Calculate the rate constant of the reaction.

B. Formation of $\ce{NO2}$

The reaction in the other direction is more important at low temperatures:

$$\ce{2 NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2 NO2(g)}$$

The following rate law was found for them:

$$v = k\cdot c(\ce{NO})^2\, c(\ce{O2})$$

4.7 Specify how the reaction rate changes when the following changes in concentration are made. (For example, write "(vi): v increases by a factor of 4")

i) $c(\ce{O2})$ is quadrupled,

ii) $c(\ce{NO})$ is quadrupled,

iii) $c(\ce{NO})$ is halved,

iv) $c(\ce{O2})$ is halved, and $c(\ce{NO})$ is quadrupled,

v) $c(\ce{NO})$ is halved, and $c(\ce{O2})$ is quadrupled.

The initial velocity of the considered reaction remains constant if the temperature is increased from $460\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and all initial concentrations are bisected.

4.8 Calculate the activation energy.

C. Radicals

The radical OH plays a vital role in the chemistry of the atmosphere. It is very unstable and short-lived. Since it reacts with many air pollutants (such as methane and ozone) and often acts as the first step in their removal, it is sometimes referred to as the "cleaning agent of the troposphere".

It can also react with $\ce{O2}$, producing the radical $\ce{HO3}$. The reaction between $\ce{O2}$ and OH has been studied in detail, and the following mechanism for the formation of $\ce{HO3}$ has been proposed:

$$\begin{array}{l} \ce{OH + O2 ->[k_1] HO3^*} \\ \ce{HO3^* ->[k_2] OH + O2} \\ \ce{HO3^* + N2 ->[k_3] HO3 + N2} \end{array}$$

$\ce{HO3^*}$ represents an excited state of $\ce{HO3}$. For the following calculations, consider $\ce{HO3^*}$ and $\ce{HO3}$ as two different chemical compounds.

4.9 Give the rate law for each elementary reaction.

4.10 Derive an equation for the rate of formation of $\ce{HO3}$. Use the steady-state approximation for all intermediate products.

4.11 The expression obtained in 4.10 becomes more straightforward if we assume that $k_2$ is negligibly small. What is the simplified expression?

Problem 6 (6 points). Structural elucidation of oriental spices

Author: St. Seywald

The history of herbs and spices goes back almost to the beginning of humankind. Among other things, caraway seeds have been found in the remains of the Neolithic (3,000 BC) lakeside settlements in Switzerland. In 2300 BC, an Egyptian tablet shows the use of cassia and thyme in beer production. Around 700 BC, a cuneiform script library of the Assyrian ruler Assurbanipal describes dill, fennel, cardamom, saffron, sesame, and thyme. Thus the following pages of the competition take their place in the ancient cultural history of the description of spices. Of course, we will not use hieroglyphics or cuneiform script to decipher the information.

A. Caraway

The main components of caraway seeds are D-(+)-Carvone (over 50%), D-(+)-Limonene (over 30%), myrcene und $\alpha$-phellandrene. D-(+)-Carvone is (S)-2-Methyl-5-(prop-1-en-2-yl)-cyclohex-2-enone.
