Problem 7 (9 points). Thermo- and quantum-chemical consideration of some B, P, and N compounds

Author: G. Schellander

Borazine

The Lewis acid $\ce{BH3}$ reacts with the Lewis base $\ce{NH3}$ to form the aminoborane $\ce{H3B-NH3}$. Organic-oriented people immediately think of the isoelectronic ethane $\ce{H3C-CH3}$. Hoping for further parallels to carbon chemistry, they are not disappointed. Borazine $\ce{B3N3H6}$ with its hexagonal backbone is also called inorganic benzene.

7.1 For borazine, draw three resonance structures with all electron pairs and any formal charges. Also use mesomeric limiting formulas that suggest the aromaticity of the structure.

The internal angles in Borazine are not quite the same, as the following sketch shows and as the correct Lewis formula suggests:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-7-fig1.png

7.2 Write the correct element symbols (N or B) for X and Y.

Boron Nitride

A further interesting compound is the boron nitride BN. It exists - like carbon itself - in several modifications. The graphite-analogous hexagonal BN (h-BN) is formed in a reaction of boric acid $\ce{H3BO3}$ (or $\ce{B(OH)3}$) and urea $\ce{CO(NH2)2}$, among others:

$$\text{Reaction 1:}\quad \ce{2 B(OH)3_{(s)} + CO(NH2)2_{(s)} -> 2 BN_{(s)} + CO2_{(g)} + 5 H2O_{(g)}}$$

Four reactions (based on boron trioxide or ammonium carbamate) and their reaction enthalpies are given at $298\,\mathrm{K}$:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{(A):} & \ce{B2O3_{(s)} + 2 NH3_{(g)} -> 2 BN_{(s)} + 3 H2O_{(g)}} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H^\ominus = 131{,}1\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \text{(B):} & \ce{B2O3_{(s)} + 3 H2O_{(g)} -> 2 B(OH)3_{(s)}} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H^\ominus = -189{,}7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \text{(C):} & \ce{H2NCOONH4_{(s)} -> 2 NH3_{(g)} + CO2_{(g)}} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H^\ominus = 157{,}2\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \text{(D):} & \ce{H2NCOONH4_{(s)} -> CO(NH2)2_{(s)} + H2O_{(g)}} & \Delta_\mathrm{R}H^\ominus = 67{,}6\,\mathrm{kJ/mol} \end{array}$$

7.3 Calculate the value $\Delta_R H^\ominus_{298}$ for reaction 1 using the given data. Show how you include reactions (A) to (D) in the calculations.

In reality, reaction 1 takes place at temperatures significantly higher than $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Here are the isobaric heat capacities:

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Compound} & C_\mathrm{p}/\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{BH3O3_{(s)}} & 86{,}1 \\ \ce{BN_{(s)}} & 19{,}7 \\ \ce{CH4N2O_{(s)}} & 94{,}0 \\ \ce{CO2_{(g)}} & 37{,}1 \\ \ce{H2O_{(g)}} & 33{,}6 \end{array}$$

7.4 Calculate $\Delta_R H^\ominus$ for reaction 1 at $900\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Graphene as a "single graphite layer" is well known. Single BN layers are also being investigated. There are similarities, but also differences. The figure below shows the structure of such a layer. The B-N bond distance is $1{,}45\,\text{Å}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-7-fig2.png

problems.title: Hydrogen – atomic, exotic and molecular
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (6 points). Hydrogen – atomic, exotic and molecular

Author: G. Schellander

Atomic hydrogen

In 1888 the Swedish physicist Johannes Rydberg presented the formula for the wavenumbers of the spectral lines in the hydrogen spectrum, which is named after him today:

$$\tilde{\nu} = R_H\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right) \qquad (1)$$

For hydrogen, the value of the Rydberg constant $R_\mathrm{H} = 109678\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The formula gives the ionization energy of the H atom in the ground state correctly ($13{,}6\,\mathrm{eV}$), as well as the wavenumbers or wavelengths of the spectral lines for various series.

A spectral series of the H atom starts at $7459{,}9\,\mathrm{nm}$ and has its shortest wavelength line at $2279{,}4\,\mathrm{nm}$.

8.1 Find the quantum number $n_1$ of this series. Provide your calculations.

8.2 Specify the wavelengths of the first three lines of this series, i.e., for (1) $n_2 = n_1 + 1$, (2) $n_2 = n_1 + 2$ and (3) $n_2 = n_1 + 3$

8.3 Indicate in which range of the electromagnetic spectrum these lines are located ($\gamma$, X-ray, UV, VIS, IR)

The Rydberg constant can be divided into two parts and thus can be generalized. It is

$$R_H = \frac{\mu_H}{m_e} R_\infty, \qquad \text{where } R_\infty = \frac{m_e e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 h^3 c} = 10973732\,\mathrm{m^{-1}} \qquad (2)$$

where $\mu_H$ is the reduced mass of the hydrogen atom (one proton and one electron), $m_\mathrm{e}$ is the electron mass, and all other natural constants have their usual meaning.

The Schrödinger equation also provides expressions for energy levels of electrons in the hydrogen atom as well as in hydrogen-like ions with the nuclear charge number $Z$ and the reduced mass $\mu$.

$$E_n = -\frac{Z^2 \mu e^4}{32\,\pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 \hbar^2 n^2} \qquad (3)$$

8.4 Show that the Rydberg formula (1) can be obtained from the relation (3) by deriving from (3) the wave number for a transition between the levels $n_1$ and $n_2$ in hydrogen ($Z = 1$).

8.5 Calculate the Rydberg constant $R_{Li}$ for the $\ce{Li^{2+}}$-Ion in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. For the mass of the Li atomic nucleus use $6{,}941\,\mathrm{u}$.

Exotic hydrogen

In so-called "exotic atoms", individual elementary particles are replaced by others. For example, in muonic hydrogen the muon $\mu$ ($m_\mu = 206{,}8\,m_\mathrm{e}$) replaces the electron. Both particles are leptons with the same charge, and for this example, we want to disregard the short life of the muon particle (approx. $2{,}2\,\mathrm{\mu s}$).

8.6 Calculate the ionization energy of the muonic H atom in kJ/mol

The wave function $\Psi_{(1,0,0)}$, i.e., the 1s orbital, shows a maximum of the radial residence probability at the radius of the first Bohr orbit $a_0$. This Bohr radius is usually given as

$$a_0 = \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m_e e^2} \qquad (4)$$

Here the atomic nucleus is neglected, otherwise the reduced mass of the system nucleus–electron would have to stand instead of the electron mass.

8.7 Which of the following expressions correctly represents the value corresponding to Bohr's radius for the muonic hydrogen? Write down the letter.

$$(A)\ \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}{m_\mu e^2} \qquad (\mathrm{B})\ \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 m_p \hbar^2}{m_\mu m_p e^2} + \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 m_\mu \hbar^2}{m_p m_\mu e^2} \qquad (\mathrm{C})\ \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}{\mu_e e^2} + \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}{\mu_p e^2}$$

Molecular hydrogen

The hydrogen molecule $\ce{H2}$ is known to be stable against dissociation which can take place in two ways:

(a) homolytic $\mathrm{H_2 \rightarrow H{\cdot} + {\cdot}H}$ (b) heterolytic $\ce{H2 -> H+ + H-}$

The diagram schematically shows the total energy of the system of two H atoms against the nuclear distance $R$. The zero-point of the energy scale corresponds to unbound protons and electrons, so atoms and molecules have the same energy scale. The two curve branches I and II represent the courses for the above-mentioned dissociations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2020-8-fig1.png

8.8 Which curve branch stands for which bond splitting? Assign (a) and (b) to the curve branches (I) and (II) correctly.

8.9 Specify the energies required for fissions (a) and (b) in eV. Neglect the zero-point energy of the $\ce{H2}$ molecule.

The homolytic cleavage (a) could also take place photolytically, in which case the photon would have to bring along the dissociation energy as minimum energy.

8.10 Does this minimum energy correspond to a minimum wavelength $\lambda_{min}$ or a maximum wavelength $\lambda_{max}$?

8.11 Calculate this $\lambda$ for the photolysis of $\ce{H2}$ in nm.

8.12 Calculate the electron affinity of the H-atom in kJ/mol from the available data. Write a positive number if the process $\ce{H + e- -> H-}$ is exothermic.

problems.problem:
Problem 1 (10 points). Iron

Author: G. Schellander

A. Bornite

Bornite, ($\ce{Cu5FeS4}$, $M = 501.88\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$), named after the Austrian Mineralogist Ignaz von Born, is an abundant mineral. Pretty crystals, however are rare. Like all sulfide ores, Bornite can be roasted, i.e. heated under oxygen supply leading to the with the formation of copper(II)oxide, iron(III)oxide, and sulfur(IV)oxide.

1.1 Write a balanced equation for roasting with integer coefficients.

When looking at the structure of bornite, one quickly encounters complicated relationships. Above $228\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a high-temperature modification ("high bornite") is stable. The sulfide ions form a cubic close packing, where Cu and Fe occupy the tetrahedral holes (TL).

1.2 To which Bravais lattice doe a cubic closed packing correspond and along which line (edge, face diagonal, space diagonal) do the atoms touch each other?

1.3 Specify the number of TL in a unit cell.

1.4 Find the fractions of TL in the unit cell that are occupied by Cu and Fe ions. Write fractions, not decimals.

The lattice constant of high bornite is $a = 5.50\,\text{Å}$.

1.5 Calculate the density of high bornite in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$

On cooling the high bornite transforms into a low-temperature modification (low bornite). The metal ions seem to keep their arrangement, but the symmetry is lost, and so low bornite can be attributed to the orthorhombic system. The density increases slightly to $5.09\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

The following structure has been proposed. The repetitive unit is a "supercell" of two cubic cells A and B:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-1-fig1.png

from left to right: Supercell, cell type A, cell type B (modified, from Canadian Mineralogist Vol 16 (1978), pp. 397-404)

In cell type A all TL are occupied, in cell type B half of the TL are occupied with Cu-ions.

1.6 Give the number of bornite formulae units in the above shown supercell.

1.7 Find the fractions of the TL in A-type cells that have to be occupied by Cu- and Fe-ions so that the correct formulae of bornite results. Write fractions., not decimals.

In fact symmetry is distorted, the aspect ratios oft he supercell are $a:b:c = 0.501:1:0.501$.

1.8 Calculate the lattice constants $a$, $b$, $c$ for low bornite.

B. Iron complexes

Numerous iron complexes are known. You certainly are familiar with the detection of iron by $\ce{SCN-}$.

1.9 Draw two Lewis structures for the thiocyanate ion, showing that this ion can coordinate with both the N and the S atom.

Below you can see four calculated molecular orbitals of the thiocyanate ion, with the S atom being on the left in each case.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-1-fig2.png

1.10 Answer the following questions by writing the letter(s) oft he correct orbital image(s) to the question number..

1) Anti-bonding between C and N is …

2) The orbital with the highest energy is …

3) The MO containing a stand-alone p-orbital of the S-atom …

4) The MO with $\pi$ – bonding over all atoms is …

5) A $\sigma$-bond is represented by ….

1.11 Sketch the two configurational isomers for $\ce{[Fe(OH2)3(SCN)3]}$ and assign the correct stereo-descriptors.

1.12 Name the complex $\ce{[Fe(OH2)3(SCN)3]}$

A salt containing hexacyanidoferrate(II) as anion consists of 43.75% N, 9.990% O, 6.308% H as well as carbon.

1.13 Calculate C-content in mass percent rounded to two decimals.

1.14 Determine the complete formulae oft the salt by calculation. Hint: Start with the iron in the anion. .

Many complexes of iron are octahedral. As it is well known, the ligands cause the splitting of the d-orbitals. In the octahedral ligand field, a distinction is made between the energetically elevated $\mathrm{e_g}$ orbitals (1) and (2) and the lowered $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals (3) - (5), which are shown here:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-1-fig3.png

1.15 Assign the standard labels to the d-orbitals (1) to (5).

The hexacyanidoferrate(II)-ion is a diamagnetic, low-spin, octahedral complex with $\Delta_\mathrm{O} = 32800\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and $P = 210\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

1.16 Write the complete (!) electron configuration fort he central atom.

1.17 Express $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$ in units of eV.

1.18 Calculate the ligand field stabilisation energy (LFSE) for the complex in eV.

Some complexes show the so-called Jahn–Teller effect: the regular octahedron is distorted into a square bipyramid by moving the atoms on the $z$-axis further from the centre. The energy levels become split even further. However, the effect only occurs, if a further enlargement of the LFSE can be achieved.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-1-fig4.png

1.19 Which of the d-orbitals is being raised or lowered? Assign the standard labels (e.g.- $\mathrm{d}_{z^2}$) to each d-orbital from (1) to (4)

Three different electron configurations for (undistorted) octahedral complexes are shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-1-fig5.png

1.20 Assign „yes“ or „no“ tot he configurations (1), (2), (3) depending on whether or not you expect a distortion by the Jahn-Teller-effect.

problems.title: Thermodynamic
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (10 points). Thermodynamic

Author: G. Schellander

A. Calcium chloride

Calcium chloride is a well-known desiccant due to the high hygroscopicity of anhydrous $\ce{CaCl2}$. It can be made by dissolving lime in hydrochloric acid:

$\ce{CaCO3_{(s)} + 2 HCl_{(aq)} -> CaCl2_{(aq)} + CO2_{(g)} + H2O_{(l)}}$. Per 50 g of $\ce{CaCO3}$, 7.3 kJ of energy are released. First, a hexahydrate is obtained from the solution. Then it is dried at standard pressure by heating to almost $300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to the anhydrous form. That requires 362 kJ of energy per mole of $\ce{CaCl2}$.

The table shows some enthalpies:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{CaCl2*6H2O_{(s)}} & \ce{H2O_{(l)}} & \ce{H2O_{(g)}} & \ce{CO2_{(g)}} & \ce{HCl_{(g)}} & \ce{HCl_{(aq)}} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ/\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & -2608 & -285.8 & -241.8 & -393.5 & -92.31 & -167.2 \end{array}$$

3.1 Calculate the enthalpy of formation for $\ce{CaCl2}$ with 1 decimal place.

Of course anhydrous $\ce{CaCl2}$ can also be produced from the elements according to the Born-Haber cycle given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-3-fig1.png

Here is a list of enthalpies most of which are given:

$$\begin{array}{c|l|r} & & \Delta H^\circ\text{-values in kJ/mol} \\ \hline (1) & \text{First ionisation energy of Ca} & 590.0 \\ (2) & \text{Second ionisation energy of Ca} & 1145.0 \\ (3) & \text{Bond dissociation enthalpy of } \ce{Cl2} & 242.6 \\ (4) & \text{Lattice energy of } \ce{CaCl2} & ? \\ (5) & \text{Negative enthalpy of formation of } \ce{CaCl2} & ? \\ (6) & \text{Sublimation enthalpy of calcium} & 177.8 \\ (7) & \text{double electron affinity of Cl (as } \Delta_\mathrm{Ea}H) & -698.0 \end{array}$$

If you did not get a value at 3.1 use $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{CaCl2}) = -1000\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

3.2 Indicate the species present at the step designated X. Do not forget indices and electric charges.

3.3 Assign the numbers of the energies (1) to (9) to the letters in the Born-Haber cycle a to h.

3.4 Calculate the lattice energy of $\ce{CaCl2}$.

B. Fritzi, entropy and humidity

The change in entropy of an ideal gas during isothermal expansion or compression can be expressed as

$$\Delta S = nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} = -\,nR\ln\frac{p_2}{p_1}$$

3.5 Prove the equivalence of the two expressions (with $V$ and $p$ respectively) for an ideal gas.

The value for the molar standard evaporation entropy ($\Delta_\mathrm{vap}S^\circ$ $109.1\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$) at 1 bar (100000 Pa) is less known than the boiling point of water (373.15 K) at 1 atm (101325 Pa). In the following, let us treat water vapour as an ideal gas.

3.6 Calculate the molar entropy change when water vapour is brought form standard pressure (1bar) to 1 atm. Give the answer with 5 significant figures.

3.7 Calculate the molar entropy of evaporation of water at 1 atm and $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Give the answer with 5 significant figures.

3.8 Calculate the enthalpy of evaporation of water $\Delta_\mathrm{vap}H_{373.15}$ Give the answer with 5 significant figures.

The process of evaporation can be described like a chemical reaction:

$$\ce{H2O_{(l)} <=> H2O_{(g)}}$$

From the standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K one can calculate a “standard enthalpy of reaction” - the standard enthalpy of evaporation $\Delta_\mathrm{vap}H^\circ_{298}$

The $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ$ values for water are taken from the previous section. $C_\mathrm{p}(\ce{H2O_{(l)}}) = 75.30\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $C_\mathrm{p}(\ce{H2O_{(g)}}) = 33.60\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$

3.9 Calculate the standard enthalpy of evaporation of water $\Delta_\mathrm{vap}H^\circ_{298}$ and the enthalpy of evaporation $\Delta_\mathrm{vap}H_{373}$ Using Kirchhoff’s law.

Little Fritzi always has problems with the respiratory tract. Frightened, his parents realize that in his bedroom ($48.6\,\mathrm{m^3}$ air volume) at $22\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, there is a relative humidity of only 38%. The saturation vapor pressure at this temperature is 2646 Pa.

3.10 Calculate the partial pressure of the water vapor in the bedroom in Pa.

The parents wet a tea towel ($40\times50\,\mathrm{cm}$), the cloth absorbs 70.0 g of water, and they hang it in Fritzi's room. After 6 hours, the cloth is dry. The pressure in the room is 1 atm. Assume that the water from the tea towel is wholly turned into humidity.

3.11 Calculate the humidity after the tea towel drying.

C. Bart and Henry

Fritzi's elder brother Bart is keen on medium-dangerous experiments. He came up with the idea of making soda water and got himself dry ice ($\ce{CO2_{(s)}}$). According to the Austrian Food Book, water must contain at least 4g/L carbon dioxide to be called soda water. To be on the safe side, Bart takes 20 g (0.500 mol) of dry ice. His room has $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (293 K) and air pressure of 1.013 bar. He finds a screw-on glass jug (1.00 L content), inserts the dry ice, and quickly screws the lid. Then he wants to get water and leaves. Luckily he is not in the room when the glass explodes after the sublimation of half of the dry ice.

3.12 Calculate the pressure in the glass immediately before the explosion in bar with two decimals.

Such mishaps do not shake Bart. To a second similar glass jug, he first adds 0.500 L of water ($\rho = 1.00\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$) and then again, the same amount (0.500 mol) of dry ice and closes it immediately. According to Henry's law (for $\ce{CO2}$ at this temperature, the Henry constant $K_{\mathrm{H}(x)} = 1.418\,\mathrm{bar}$), some of the $\ce{CO2}$ now dissolves in water, thus, saving Bart from a second explosion.

In the following, neglect any protolysis reactions of $\ce{CO2}$ in the water, the change in the amount of liquid by the dissolved $\ce{CO2}$, the air dissolved in water, and the volume of solid $\ce{CO2}$.

3.13 Calculate the amount of substance of air in the sealed vessel.

problems.title: Kinetics of Epoixides
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (7 points). Kinetics of Epoixides

Author: J. Novacek

A. Dehydrochlorination of Bisphenol A-Chlorohydrinethers

In the synthesis of epoxy resins, bisphenol A is converted with epichlorohydrin to ($\mathbf{A}$). At the end of synthesis, excess epichlorohydrin is distilled off and still contained in ($\mathbf{A}$) chlorine is separated by dehydrochlorination so as not to exceed a chlorine content of 0.1% in the product. Dehydrochlorination is carried out in two stages with sodium hydroxide.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-4-fig1.png

The following values were recorded when determining the reaction rate:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} t\,/\,\mathrm{min} & 0 & 1 & 5 & 10 & 20 & 40 & 60 \\ \hline [\mathrm{A}]\,/\,\mathrm{mol/L} & 1.000 & 0.3400 & 0.0940 & 0.0490 & 0.0252 & 0.0128 & 0.0086 \\ \ln[\mathrm{A}] & 0.000 & -1.079 & -2.364 & -3.016 & -3.681 & -4.358 & -4.756 \\ 1/[\mathrm{A}] & 1.000 & 2.941 & 10.64 & 20.41 & 39.68 & 78.13 & 116.3 \end{array}$$

4.1 Draw a diagram that shows the decrease of [A] versus time (in min). Use: 1 min … 0.25 cm, 1 mol/L … 10 cm

4.2 Determine the reaction order of this reaction. You can do this graphically or mathematically, but you have to show your approach. If you proceed mathematically show the correspondence to the rate law for at least three data points.

4.3 Write the differential rate law and report the value of rate constant $k$ (to one decimal place) with appropriate units.

4.4 From 4.3 derive an expression for half-half life $\tau$.

Dehydrochlorination takes place according to the following mechanism:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-4-fig2.png

The apparent rate constant can be expressed as:

$$k_{app} = \frac{k_1\cdot k_2}{k_{-1}\cdot[\ce{H2O}] + k_2}$$

4.5 Indicate whether the following statements are true (W) or false (F) by writing the number of the question on your answer sheet and then (W) or (F)

[W stands for German "wahr" = true.]

1) From the dependence of $k_{app}$ on the water concentration one can deduce the ratio of the individual rate constants to one another

2) If $k_2 \gg k_{-1}$, $k_{app}$ can be approximated by $k_2$.

3) If the concentration of water is increased $k_{app}$ can be approximated as $\frac{k_1\cdot k_2}{k_{-1}}$.

4) If $k_{app}$ is independent of the concentration of water, $k_{app}$ can be approximated by $k_1$.

5) If $k_{-1} \gg k_2$ $k_{app}$ decreases linearly with the concentration of water.

B. Conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ into Cyclic Carbonates

One of the challenges in using $\ce{CO2}$ as a starting material for the synthesis of organic compounds is its fixation. One possibility for this is the reaction with epoxides to form cyclic carbonates (or polycarbonates).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-4-fig3.png

[German labels in the scheme: "Katalysator" = catalyst, "cyclische Carbonate" = cyclic carbonates.]

With catalyst A, a dependence of the reaction rate on the substrate concentration is obtained, which is shown in the following diagram. A non-linear course can be seen. However, a linear approximation can be made at low substrate concentrations and at very high ones.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-4-fig4.png

[German axis labels: "Geschwindigkeit" = rate, "Substratkonz" = substrate concentration.]

4.6 By reactions of which order can one approximate this curve at (a) low and (b) very high substrate concentrations.

4.7 Name the approximation model that is usually used to explain the above shown reaction kinetics.

The rate constant $k_{app}$ was measured at different temperatures:

$$k_{app.35^\circ\mathrm{C}} = 2.83\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}} \qquad k_{app.65^\circ\mathrm{C}} = 1.11\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$$

4.8 Calculate the activation energy of the reaction in $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

If the same reaction is carried out with catalyst B, then a kinetic model with product inhibition (see figure) must be assumed in order to be able to approximate the experimental values well.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2021-4-fig5.png

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{S + Cat} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CatS}\\ \mathrm{CatS} &\rightarrow \mathrm{P + Cat}\\ \mathrm{Cat + P} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CatP} \end{aligned}$$

4.9 Write the differential rate laws for [S], [P], [Cat], [CatS] , and [CatP].

problems.title: Hydrogen Cyanide HCN
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (11 points). Hydrogen Cyanide HCN

Author: W. Faber

Hydrogen cyanide (hydrocyanic acid, $\ce{HCN}$) is produced via the Degussa-BMA process based on ammonia ($\ce{NH3}$) and methane ($\ce{CH4}$). As a by-product, elemental hydrogen is formed in this reaction.

6.1 Write a balanced equation for the hydrogen cyanide production.

6.2 Formulate the law of mass action for this reaction.

The reaction is carried out at $1250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In equilibrium the gaseous reaction mixture has a pressure of 1.00 bar and contains 71.8% hydrogen, 22.9% hydrogen cyanide, 2.5% ammonia, 1.7% methane and 1.1% nitrogen (all % $V/V$).

6.3 Calculate the equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{p}$ for the reaction using the data given.

One can also calculate the equilibrium constant from thermodynamic data of the gaseous starting materials and end products of this reaction.

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} & \Delta_f H^\ominus\ (\mathrm{kJ/mol}) & \Delta_f S^\ominus\ (\mathrm{J/K\cdot mol}) \\ \hline \text{Methane} & -74.6 & 186.3 \\ \text{Ammonia} & -45.9 & 192.8 \\ \text{Hydrogen cyanide} & 135.1 & 201.8 \\ \text{Hydrogen} & 0 & 130.7 \end{array}$$

6.4 Calculate the standard Gibbs-energy of the reaction at $1250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using these thermodynamical data.

6.5 Calculate the equilibrium constant from the calculated Gibbs-energy. State possible reasons for the difference to the result from 6.3.

Hydrogen cyanide or sodium cyanide play an important role in the extraction of silver and gold. For this process called "cyanide leaching", a solution of sodium cyanide is used.

6.6 10.00 g $\ce{NaCN}$ are dissolved in 1.00 L of water. In the solution a concentration of $2.251\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ of hydrogen cyanide is measured. Calculate the pH of this solution and the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A}$-value of hydrogen cyanide. Neglect the self ionisation of water.

The following standard potentials are given:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Ag+ + e- <=> Ag} & E^\ominus = 0.799\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{[Ag(CN)2]- + e- <=> Ag + 2 CN-} & E^\ominus = -0.31\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{O2 + 2 H2O + 4 e- <=> 4 OH-} & E^\ominus = 0.401\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

6.7 Calculate the formation constant for the $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]-}$ - complex at 298 K corresponding to the equation: $\ce{Ag+ + 2 CN- <=> [Ag(CN)2]-}$.

In cyanide leaching, the silver ore dissolves according to the following equation:

$$\ce{2 Ag + 4 NaCN + 1/2 O2 + H2O <=> 2 Na[Ag(CN)2] + 2 NaOH}$$

6.8 Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.

The cyanide concentration in a solution was historically determined by an argentometric titration developed by Justus v. Liebig. The cyanide solution is titrated with a silver(I) nitrate solution. First the silver(I) ions form the complex $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]-}$. When all cyanide ions are bound in the complex, further addition of silver(I) ions leads to the formation of solid $\ce{AgCN}$ and thus to turbidity of the solution. The solubility product of silver(I) cyanide is $5.97\cdot10^{-17}$. If you have not received a result for the complex formation constant in 6.7, use $K_\mathrm{f} = 10^{20}$.

6.9 10.00 g $\ce{NaCN}$ are dissolved in 1.00 litre of water. 10.00 mL of this solution are titrated with silver(I) nitrate solution ($c = 0.100\,\mathrm{mol/L}$). Calculate the required volume of silver nitrate solution up to the moment when the precipitation of $\ce{AgCN}$ starts. For now, assume that the formation of the complex is complete and irreversible. Assume further that acid-base-reactions of the cyanide ions can be neglected.

6.10 Now calculate the concentration of silver(I) ions in the titrated solution when the precipitation of $\ce{AgCN}$ starts. This time take the equilibrium of complex formation into account. Still assume that acid-base-reactions of cyanide can be neglected.

problems.title: Molecules with multiple bonds
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (8.5 points). Molecules with multiple bonds

Author: G. Schellander

A. Three small molecules

From the example of three diatomic molecules assembled from O and N atoms, one can learn a lot about bonding models and model building in general.

Probably the simplest way to explain bonds with the help of electrons are valence formulas according to Lewis. Unfortunately, the simplest way is not always the correct one. Because the Lewis formulas predict an unpaired electron only for one of the three molecules, and even there only because there is no other way.

1.1 Draw complete Lewis formulas for $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{O2}$, and $\ce{NO}$ showing that only one of the molecules should have an unpaired electron.

The number of paired or unpaired electrons determines whether a molecule is diamagnetic or paramagnetic. Since the experiment shows that two of the molecules mentioned are paramagnetic, one must take another step forward and consider molecular orbitals.

1.2 The following graph shows empty MO schemes. Label them, fill the MO levels with electrons, indicate the bond order for each molecule, and determine whether it should be dia- or paramagnetic.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig1.png

B. A medium-sized molecular ion

The dichromate anion $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ is well known from analytical chemistry. The covalent framework is symmetrical, which is why we will only consider the left part (with a negative charge) in the following and abbreviate the right part with X.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig2.png

1.3 Indicate which molecular geometry you expect according to VSEPR for (a) the Cr atom (b) the O atom number 4.

1.4 Draw three mesomeric (resonance) Lewis formulas of the left part showing that three of the Cr-O bonds are equivalent. Use the abbreviation X. Draw the "flipping" of the electron pairs using appropriate arrows.

1.5 In the dichromate two different Cr-O bond distances are measured: $179\,\mathrm{pm}$ and $163\,\mathrm{pm}$. Which of the bond distances do you expect for (a) the bond Cr-O$^4$, and (b) the bond Cr-O$^3$?

1.6 Give the complete electron configuration for (a) chromium (6 unpaired spins) (b) chromium(III).

C. An even larger molecule

Retinal is the chromophore in light-sensitive proteins, especially in rhodopsin, which also gives our retina its light sensitivity. A look at the structure reveals an extended $\pi$-electron system.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig3.png

[Abbildung 1 = Figure 1, Abbildung 2 = Figure 2.]

Let us first look at the molecule (derived from the middle section of retinal) drawn in Fig. 2 (Abbildung 2, right).

1.7 Name the molecule (Fig. 2) according to IUPAC including all required stereodescriptors.

Below you can see 6 calculated molecular orbitals of this molecule. The molecule is always in the same position as drawn above.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig4.png

1.8 From which of the four directions drawn in Figure 2 is the molecule viewed? Indicate the number.

1.9 Order molecular orbitals from Figure 3 by increasing energy.

1.10 Indicate for (A) and for (F) whether they are $\sigma$- or $\pi$- molecular orbitals.

1.11 One of the MOs shown is the HOMO, one is the LUMO. Indicate the corresponding letters.

In the usual representation of the all-trans-retinal in textbooks, one could fall for the idea to consider almost all $\pi$-electrons as particles in the (potential) box. A molecular model program kindly provides also the length of the potential box.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig5.png

1.12 Indicate the number of $\pi$-electrons in this box.

1.13 Calculate the wavelength of the HOMO-LUMO transition in the model of the particle in the box in nm.

1.14 Indeed, all-trans-retinal dissolved in hexane shows an extinction maximum at $380\,\mathrm{nm}$. One might think that the potential box considered here is (a) too short or (b) too long. Indicate the correct letter.

All-trans-retinol is obtained by reduction of the carbonyl group, which leads to a change in the $\pi$-electron system. Its absorption maximum is shifted by about $55\,\mathrm{nm}$ in one direction compared to that of all-trans-retinal ($\lambda_\mathrm{max} = 380\,\mathrm{nm}$). One of the curves shown on the right belongs to retinal, the other to retinol.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig6.png

1.15 Indicate the number of curve (I) or (II) belonging to the all-trans retinol.

1.16 What wavelength corresponds to the distance between two adjacent bars on the abscissa (x-axis)? (a) $5\,\mathrm{nm}$ (b) $10\,\mathrm{nm}$ (c) $15\,\mathrm{nm}$ (d) $20\,\mathrm{nm}$ (e) $25\,\mathrm{nm}$. Indicate the correct letter.

1.17 Which values should be written at $x$ and $y$? Give them in nm.

The molar decadic absorption coefficient of all-trans-retinol at the absorption maximum was determined to be $\varepsilon = 52700\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$.

1.18 Calculate the concentration of a sample whose absorbance in a $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ cell is $A = 0.445$.

D. Aromatic?!

Benzene is known to obey the Hückel rule, according to which the number of $\pi$-electrons should be 2, 6, 10, ... Other ring-shaped molecule(s) can also exhibit aromatic stability according to this rule. Nine aromatic structures are shown, with either the number of $\pi$-electrons or the charge indicated for each.

1.19 Complete the formulas by writing the number of $\pi$-electrons in an empty circle or the charge in an empty box. Also write 0 (zero) explicitly.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-1-fig7.png

Borazine $\ce{B3N3H6}$ has sometimes been nicknamed "inorganic benzene", since it also has a very nice hexagonal shape (but only with a triple axis of rotation).

1.20 Draw three mesomeric (resonance) formulas of borazine (with formal charges and lone pairs) showing that the B-N bonds are equal. One of the boundary formulas doesn't contain any multiple bonds.

B. Synthesis of cantharidin

Stork, G.; van Tamelen, E. E.; Friedman, L. J.; Burgstahler, A. W. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1951, 73, 4501.

Cantharidin is a terpenoid that beetles secrete as a defensive secretion or sex pheromone, depending on the species. Today it is known that it is a strong poison, although it is said to have an effect as an aphrodisiac. According to war reports, this has already been the undoing of Napoleon's troops in Egypt. The soldiers fed on frogs, which in turn ate beetles, which could have led to a bioaccumulation of the poison in the food chain. In the following, the synthesis of cantharidin published by the Belgian J. Stork in 1951 is considered in more detail.

C. Self-splicing of proteins

Do we owe our existence to the protein-rich beans that were mainly responsible for our ancestors not starving in Europe? The importance of beans for the ancient Romans is shown by the fact that four of the most important Roman families are named after legumes (so-called Fabaceae): Fabius (after the fava bean), Lentulus (after the lentil), Piso (after the pea), and Cicero (after the chickpea). Unfortunately, with the fall of the Roman Empire, the knowledge about the importance of these legumes disappeared. Only later the bean regained its important place in nutrition.

Protein "self-splicing" was first discovered in 1990. Thioester intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ is formed in the process. Nowadays, it is also used in peptide synthesis.

problems.title: Thermodynamics in the Solvay process
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (6 points). Thermodynamics in the Solvay process

Author: G. Schellander

A. Solvay process

Starting materials for the synthesis of soda ash (sodium carbonate) are sodium chloride and calcium carbonate. Unfortunately, the reaction in aqueous solution takes place just in the wrong direction, namely like this:

$$\ce{Na2CO3 + CaCl2 <=> 2 NaCl + CaCO3} \qquad \text{R1}$$

A way out is provided by a multi-stage implementation shown in the following scheme. It was developed by Earnest Solvay. The circles represent reactions, the substances are represented by their formulas in boxes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2022-3-fig1.png

3.1 Write down coordinated equations for reactions 1, 2, 3 and 4 and show by appropriate addition of these that the overall reaction of the Solvay process corresponds to the desired reaction (reverse reaction of R1).

3.2 You might have noticed that one arrow is missing in the above diagram. From where to where should it be drawn? ("From... to ...")

$$\begin{array}{l|r|r|r|r} & \Delta_\mathrm{f} H^\circ/\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & \Delta_\mathrm{f} G^\circ/\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & S^\circ/\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & C_p/\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{H2(g)} & 0{,}0 & & 130{,}7 & 28{,}80 \\ \ce{H2O(g)} & -241{,}8 & (\mathbf{A}) & 188{,}8 & 33{,}60 \\ \ce{O2(g)} & 0{,}0 & & 205{,}2 & 29{,}40 \\ \ce{CHNaO3(s)} & -950{,}8 & (\mathbf{B}) & 101{,}7 & 87{,}60 \\ \ce{CNa2O3(s)} & -1131 & -1045 & 138{,}9 & 112{,}3 \\ \ce{CO2(g)} & -393{,}5 & -394{,}4 & 213{,}8 & 37{,}10 \end{array}$$

Thermodynamic data from the CRC Handbook

A crucial step in the process is the thermal decomposition of the sodium hydrogen carbonate:

$$\ce{2 NaHCO3(s) <=> Na2CO3(s) + H2O(g) + CO2(g)} \qquad \text{R2}$$

At $298\,\mathrm{K}$ the value for the equilibrium constant for this reaction (R2) is $K_p = 1.016\cdot10^{-6}$.

3.3 Give the expression for the equilibrium constant $K_p$.

3.3 Calculate $\Delta_R G^\circ_{298}$.

3.5 Calculate the two missing quantities ($\mathbf{A}$) and ($\mathbf{B}$) in the table.

In the industrial process, the reaction is carried out at $180\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($453\,\mathrm{K}$). At this temperature, the saturation vapor pressure of water is already $1001.9\,\mathrm{kPa}$, which means that condensation begins as soon as the partial pressure of water exceeds this pressure.

3.4 Calculate $K_p$ at $453\,\mathrm{K}$, assume $\Delta_R H^\circ$ to be constant.

3.5 Calculate the equilibrium partial pressure $p_{\ce{CO2}}$ above the just dry reaction mixture at this temperature, i. e. when the water vapor has reached its saturation pressure.

Let's turn our attention to future ventures of mankind on other planets. How about a Solvay plant on Venus for example? The working conditions would be exciting: The atmosphere contains only 20 ppm $\ce{H2O}$ but 96.5% (V/V) $\ce{CO2}$ and the whole thing at a total pressure of $p_\mathrm{ges} = 92\,\mathrm{bar}$. In addition, the average temperature is $737\,\mathrm{K}$.

[$p_\mathrm{ges}$: "ges" (German "gesamt") = total.]

3.6 Calculate $\Delta_R H^\circ$ and $\Delta_R S^\circ$ of reaction R2 on Venus, consider $C_p$ to be independent of temperature.

3.7 Determine by calculation whether $\ce{NaHCO3}$ decomposes spontaneously on Venus according to equation R2.

The reaction of cesium with chlorine gas is strongly exothermic. The standard enthalpy of formation of cesium chloride is $-443\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Below more physical data around cesium and chlorine are given:

$$\begin{array}{lrl} \text{Sublimation enthalpy of Cs:} & +78.0 & \mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \text{1. ionization energy of Cs:} & 3.89 & \mathrm{eV} \\ \text{2. ionization energy of Cs:} & 23.16 & \mathrm{eV} \\ \text{Dissociation energy of } \ce{Cl2}\text{:} & 243 & \mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \text{Electron affinity of Cl:} & 3.62 & \mathrm{eV}\ \text{(Attention "stupid sign")} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Formation and decay of hydrogen iodide
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (4.5 points). Formation and decay of hydrogen iodide

Author: J. Novacek

Bodenstein carried out kinetics measurements on hydrogen iodide at the end of the 19th century. He concluded that both formation and decay represent a bimolecular reaction and was also able to determine the activation energies for the formation and decay of hydrogen iodide.

$$(1) \qquad \ce{H2 + I2 <=> 2 HI}$$

$$E_\mathrm{A,formation} = 167\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}, \quad E_\mathrm{A,decay} = 184\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$$

6.1 The decay of hydrogen iodide corresponds to a reaction of: (Tick correctly!)

• 0th order
• 1st order
• 2nd order

The following measurement values were obtained at $556\,\mathrm{K}$:

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l|l|l} t\,/\,\mathrm{h} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 5 \\ \hline [\mathrm{HI}]\,/\,\mathrm{mol/mL} & 1{,}000 & 0{,}441 & 0{,}283 & 0{,}136 \\ \hline \ln[\mathrm{HI}] & 0{,}000 & -0{,}817 & -1{,}261 & -1{,}991 \\ \hline 1/[\mathrm{HI}] & 1{,}000 & 2{,}265 & 3{,}531 & 7{,}328 \end{array}$$

6.2 Using a graph, show that the assumption of a bimolecular reaction does not contradict the given measured values. Make sure that the axes are labeled correctly.

6.3 Indicate (with sign) by what percentage the initial concentration must be changed to achieve a doubling of the reaction rate.

6.4 Determine the reaction rate constant (with 3 significant digits) and write it down with the corresponding unit.

6.5 Calculate the rate constant for the decay at $720\,\mathrm{K}$.

Later investigations have shown that the formation of hydrogen iodide is not quite as simple as originally assumed. It could be shown that the following elementary reactions play a role in the formation of hydrogen iodide.

$$\begin{array}{ll} (2) & \ce{I2 <=>[$k_2$][$k_{-2}$] 2 I} \\ (3) & \ce{I + H2 <=>[$k_3$][$k_{-3}$] IH2} \\ (4) & \ce{I + IH2 ->[$k_4$] 2 HI} \end{array}$$

6.6 Establish the differential velocity laws for $[\mathrm{HI}]$ and $[\mathrm{IH_2}]$.

Reactions (2) and (3) are very fast upstream equilibria, that is, $k_4 \ll k_{-2}$, $k_{-3}$ and the concentrations occurring in the equilibria can be determined using the corresponding equilibrium constants.

6.7 Express $[\mathrm{IH_2}]$ using the equilibrium constants $K_2$ and $K_3$ and the concentrations of $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ and $[\mathrm{I_2}]$.

Under the condition of upstream equilibria, the reaction rate for the formation of hydrogen iodide (1) can be described as follows:

$$v = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[HI]}{dt} = k_{tot}\cdot[H_2]^a\cdot[I_2]^b$$

6.8 Determine the reaction orders $a$ and $b$ and give the relationship between $k_{tot}$ and the rate constants of the partial steps.

Problem 7 (10.5 points). Equilibria of mercury

Author: W. Faber

Assume that $0.0500\,\mathrm{g}$ of mercury(II) oxide dissolves completely in $1.00$ liter of water.

7.1 Write the equation for the reaction of mercury(II) oxide with water and calculate the pH of the resulting solution.

In compounds, mercury can occur divalent (as $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ ion) and monovalent. The monovalent mercury is always present as a diatomic cluster; therefore, the ion is written in the form $\ce{Hg2^{2+}}$. The salts have corresponding formulas such as $\ce{Hg2Cl2}$ and $\ce{Hg2I2}$.

Given are the reduction potentials at pH = 0:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Hg^{2+} + e- <=> 1/2 Hg2^{2+}} & E^\ominus = 0.911\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{1/2 Hg2^{2+} + e- <=> Hg} & E^\ominus = 0.796\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

7.2 Calculate the reduction potential for the reaction $\ce{Hg^{2+} + 2e- <=> Hg}$.

The mercury(I) ion can also disproportionate: $\ce{Hg2^{2+} <=> Hg^{2+} + Hg}$.

7.3 Using the reduction potentials given, calculate the equilibrium constant for the disproportionation reaction.

A mercury(II) nitrate solution ($0.0100\,\mathrm{mol/L}$) reacts with an excess of elemental mercury.

7.4 Using the result from the previous example, calculate the concentrations of $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Hg2^{2+}}$ in this solution. If you have not obtained a result for the equilibrium constant, use the value $K = 0.012$.

The solubility product of $\ce{Hg2F2}$ is $3.10\cdot10^{-6}$.

7.5 Calculate the standard potential for the reaction $\ce{Hg2F2 + 2e- <=> 2 Hg + 2 F-}$.

To $1.00$ liter of a mercury(II) nitrate solution ($0.0100\,\mathrm{mol/L}$), $1.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of solid NaOH is added. Two different complexes are formed, whose complex formation constants are given below:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{[Hg(OH)]+} & \beta_1 = 2.00\cdot10^{10} \\ \ce{[Hg(OH)2]} & \beta_2 = 5.01\cdot10^{21} \end{array}$$

For the following calculations, assume that no precipitate forms and that there is no change in the oxidation state of mercury.

7.6 Calculate the pH of the resulting solution and the concentrations of all mercury species present in the solution. If simplifying assumptions have to be made, then these are to be checked with the results for their reasonableness.

problems.title: Applications of lithium
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (8 points). Applications of lithium

Author: W. Faber

A. Lithium rechargeable batteries

In technically used lithium rechargeable batteries, the negative electrode usually consists of lithium embedded in a graphite structure. The positive electrode can be made of different materials. In the case of lithium-ion batteries, it is usually made of lithium cobalt(III) oxide, while in the case of lithium iron phosphate batteries, the positive electrode consists of lithium iron(II) phosphate.

Reactions involved:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{(C)_{n} + Li+ + e- <=> Li(C)_{n}} & E^\circ = -3.05\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{CoO2 + Li+ + e- <=> LiCoO2} & E^\circ = +0.19\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{FePO4 + Li+ + e- <=> LiFePO4} & E^\circ = +0.35\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

1.1 Write down the overall chemical equation for discharging a lithium iron phosphate battery and calculate the standard potential difference for this reaction.

The lithium iron phosphate battery achieves in practice a maximum energy density of $160\,\mathrm{Wh\times kg^{-1}}$.

1.2 Calculate what percentage of the theoretically possible maximum energy density was thus achieved. Assume a value of $n = 6$ for this calculation.

For the production of a lithium iron phosphate battery, among other things, an aluminium carrier foil is used to which a thin layer of lithium iron(II) phosphate is applied on one side. The carrier foil has a thickness of $15.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, the lithium iron(II) phosphate layer a thickness of $68.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. The purity of the lithium iron(II) phosphate used is 93%, the density is $1765\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. The film has a format of $241\,\mathrm{mm} \times 200\,\mathrm{mm}$.

1.3 Calculate the maximum capacity of such a film in milliampere hours mAh.

B. Lithium carbonate

Lithium carbonate ($M = 73.89\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) is significantly less soluble than the carbonates of the other alkali metals. At $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the solubility is $13.3\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$, at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ $7.2\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$.

1.4 Calculate the molar enthalpy of solution of lithium carbonate. Assume that the enthalpy is constant in the temperature interval considered.

C. Lithium hydroxide

In the Apollo space program, lithium hydroxide was used to remove the exhaled carbon dioxide from the air.

1.5 Give a balanced chemical equation for the reaction of lithium hydroxide with carbon dioxide.

1.6 Calculate the maximum volume of carbon dioxide gas that can be bound by $1.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of pure lithium hydroxide at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$ pressure.

Lithium hydroxide reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in the air to form lithium carbonate. Its purity can be determined via titration. For this purpose, a first titration first carried out with $\ce{HCl}$ and methyl orange, whereby both lithium hydroxide and lithium carbonate react. In a second titration, an excess of barium chloride is first added to precipitate the carbonate. Then $\ce{HCl}$ is used again to titrate the hydroxide using phenolphthalein as an indicator.

The sample is a mixture of lithium hydroxide and lithium carbonate. To prepare a stock solution, $2.500\,\mathrm{g}$ of this mixture are transferred to a $500\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask, dissolved in water, filled up and homogenized. Then $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of this stock solution is titrated with $\ce{HCl}$ ($0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) and methyl orange, consuming $48.5\,\mathrm{mL}$ to the equivalence point. Barium chloride is added to another $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the stock solution until no precipitate is formed. The following titration with $\ce{HCl}$ ($0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) and phenolphthalein as indicator results in a consumption of $41.7\,\mathrm{mL}$.

1.7 Calculate the masses of lithium hydroxide and lithium carbonate in this sample.

In order to be able to estimate the accuracy of this titration method, you should now perform the following calculation:

Assume to have a carbonate concentration of $0.0100\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ in the $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ sample solution. Add $3.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a barium chloride solution with a concentration of $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$. The solubility product of barium carbonate is $2.58\times10^{-9}$.

1.8 Calculate the concentration of carbonate ions in the solution after the addition of the barium chloride.

A second titration method for the given mixture starts with the same titration with $\ce{HCl}$ and methyl orange as indicator as the first method. However, the second titration is carried out with $\ce{HCl}$ and an indicator which has its transition point at a pH value of 8.2.

1.9 Give the ionic equation for the reaction of the carbonate ion in the second titration.

The indicator methyl orange is synthetically accessible by azo coupling:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2023-1-fig1.png

1.10 Draw the constitutional formulas of the reactants and give the sum formulas of the reagents leading to this indicator. Name the type of reaction in the above coupling.

Problem 4 (7.5 points). Some thermodynamics of NOx

Author: G. Schellander

Since the oxygen source for combustion processes usually is air, nitrogen inevitably also enters the respective combustion chamber. Thus, equilibria of for the formation of nitrogen oxides have to be considered:

$$\ce{N2_{(g)} + O2_{(g)} <=> 2 NO_{(g)}} \qquad \mathbf{R1}$$

In the following tasks let us assume that only NO is formed and that no other nitrogen oxides are produced.

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|} \hline & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ/\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & S^\circ/\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & C_p/\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{N2_{(g)}} & 0.0 & 191.6 & 29.1 \\ \hline \ce{NO_{(g)}} & 91.3 & 210.8 & 29.9 \\ \hline \ce{O2_{(g)}} & 0.0 & 205.2 & 29.40 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Thermodynamische Daten aus dem CRC-Handbook

4.1 Determine $\Delta_\mathrm{R}G^\circ_{298}$ and $K_p$ (at $298\,\mathrm{K}$) for the reaction ($\mathbf{R1}$).

4.2 Determine $\Delta_\mathrm{f}G^\circ$ of nitrogen(II) oxide.

Let us assume in the following that $\Delta_\mathrm{R}H^\circ$, and $\Delta_\mathrm{R}S^\circ$ are temperature independent. It is known that:

$$K_p = \frac{p_{NO}^2}{p_{O_2} \times p_{N_2}}$$

4.3 Derive an expression from $K_p$ that gives $p_{NO}$ as a function of $T$, $p_{O2}$, $p_{N2}$, $\Delta_R H^\circ$ and $\Delta_R S^\circ$.

4.4 Based on your previous results, tick the correct answers:

With increasing temperature

• $p_\mathrm{NO}$ increases.
• $p_\mathrm{NO}$ decreases.

The correctly derived expression for $p_\mathrm{NO}$ as a function of temperature can be represented as a linear function:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2023-4-fig1.png

4.5 For this graph, give the correct expressions for ….

… labeling of the ordinate (y-axis):

… labeling of the abscissa (x-axis):

… slope:

… ordinate section (section on the y-axis)

Since nitrogen oxides are known to be environmental pollutants (next to a few other hazards), attempts are being made to keep their emission low by removing them from the exhaust gas stream after combustion. One method of doing this is selective catalytic reduction (SCR), in which nitrogen monoxide reacts with ammonia at elevated temperatures to produce nitrogen.

4.6 Give a balanced chemical equation for this reaction including the states of matter.

The reaction is faster if the exhaust gas stream contains nitrogen dioxide in addition to nitrogen monoxide. The reaction is often written like this:

Problem 5 (12 points). Copper-64

Author: G. Schellander, J. Novacek

Throughout this problem use the scientific notation for numbers above 1000 and below 0.001.

Copper-64 can be prepared by various methods. By thermal neutrons in an (n, $\gamma$)-reaction, by fast neutrons in an (n, p)-reaction or in a cylcotron (accelerator for charged particles) by a (p, n)-reaction.

5.1 Specify the starting nuclides in each case.

$\underline{\qquad}$ (n, $\gamma$) $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ $\qquad$ $\underline{\qquad}$ (n, p) $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ $\qquad$ $\underline{\qquad}$ (p, n) $\ce{^{64}Cu}$

$\ce{^{64}Cu}$ can also be generated from natural zinc in a cyclotron. For this purpose, a (d, 2p)-reaction is used. Natural zinc consists of the stable isotopes $\ce{^{64}Zn}$, $\ce{^{66}Zn}$, $\ce{^{67}Zn}$, $\ce{^{68}Zn}$ with proportions of 49.2%, 27.7%, 4.00%, 18.5%).

5.2 Give a balanced nuclear chemical equation (with all atomic and mass numbers) for this process.

In an experiment, a $15\,\mathrm{MeV}$ deuteron beam (i.e. a beam of $\ce{^{2}H+}$ ions) was able to achieve a yield of $1.195\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{Bq\,\mu A^{-1}\,h^{-1}}$. Assume that the Zn target had a mass of $5\,\mathrm{mg}$ and that 1.00 % of the target were actually hit by the deuteron beam. Use the molar mass of Zn from the periodic table; the decay constant of $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ is $\lambda = 1.516\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

5.3 For irratiotion $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol}$ of deuterons are used. Calculate the fraction of the Zn nuclide (considered for conversion) that was actually converted.

$\ce{^{64}Cu}$ can decay in various ways:

• $\beta^-$-decay, (38.48 %, $E_{\max,\beta^-} = 579\,\mathrm{keV}$) – daughter isotope $\mathbf{X}$
• $\beta^+$-decay (17.52%, $E_{\max\,\beta^+}$) – daughter isotope $\mathbf{Y}$
• $\varepsilon$ electron capture ($329\,\mathrm{keV}$, 0.47%) to an excited state $\mathbf{Y}^*$

5.5 Note what has to be written in the fields 1, 2 and 3, orientate yourself for this on the already given $\varepsilon$-decay. In particular, calculate the maximum energy $E_{\beta^+}$ of the $\beta^+$ decay. Do not forget the particle(s) whose mass energy corresponds to the field 4.

Due to its positron emission, $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ has recently been used as a radioactive pharmakon for positron emission tomography (PET). For this purpose, it is bound by a multidentate ligand ("DOTA"). The ligand is attached to a small polypeptide designed to allow binding to somatostatin receptors.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2023-5-fig2.png

A table also indicates the decrease of activity to the attending physicians, because the usability is of course of limited duration.

5.7 Calculate the number of positrons emitted per second per mL of substance 9 hours after the time of production.

A patient is treated with $3\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the above given substance, PET is performed, he is allowed to go home and radioactivity continues to decrease

5.8 Calculate the time (in days) after which the activity in the patient has decreased to 0.5% of the initial value. Assume that 7% of the administered $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ is excreted during this time.

Problem 6 (2.5 points). About the structure of uronic acids

Author: J. Novacek

A. Absolute configuration of $\alpha$-L-iduronic acid

NMR spectroscopy is a very powerful method in structure elucidation. From the number of signals, their chemical shifts and their coupling patterns, a lot of information can already be gained about the structure of a compound. Another important contribution to structure elucidation - especially for "more rigid" structural elements such as double bonds or ring structures - is provided by the magnitude of the coupling constant.

The coupling constant of vicinal coupling $^{3}J$ correlates with the dihedral angle $\Phi$ according to the Karplus curve shown in the diagram below (named after its discoverer, the Vienna-born US Nobel laureate Martin Karplus).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2023-6-fig1.png

The coupling constants were measured and averaged for several $\alpha$-O-substituted L-iduronic acids. It was found that these compounds exist in three different conformations that are in equilibrium with each other. Two of these conformations (named $^{1}\mathrm{C}_4$ and $^{4}\mathrm{C}_1$) are chair conformations, while the third conformation ($^{2}\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{O}$) is a twist boat conformation.

For the $^{4}\mathrm{C}_1$ conformation the following coupling constants have been measured:

$$J_{12} = 8.0\,\mathrm{Hz};\ J_{23} = 9.7\,\mathrm{Hz},\ J_{34} = 9.0\,\mathrm{Hz},\ J_{45} = 4.8\,\mathrm{Hz}$$

Uronic acids are formed by oxidation of the primary hydroxyl group of monosaccharides.

In July 2022 media reported: "Pharmacies in Germany are currently struggling with supply shortages of medicines for children. This might give you the idea of using proven synthesis knowledge to start your own preparative work. In this assignment, you will deal with the synthesis of ibuprofen ($\ce{C13H18O2}$) – at least on paper.

Sertraline is considered a model substance (and reference) for this transport. The induced activity of the ATPase follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics.

$$v = \frac{v_{max} \cdot [S]}{K_M + [S]}$$

Robert B. Woodward was one of the most important synthesis chemists. In the 1960s, for example, he developed the synthesis of vitamin B12 with A. Eschenmoser (ETH-Zurich). With R. Hoffmann, he applied electron theory to synthetic problems. 1st experiment: $10.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of the salt were dissolved in $1.000\,\mathrm{L}$ of water. Then $10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of hydrochloric acid with a concentration of $3.000\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ was added. The resulting solution had a pH value of $\mathrm{pH} = 4.7903$.

2nd experiment: $10.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of the salt were dissolved in $1.000\,\mathrm{L}$ of water. Then $15.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of hydrochloric acid with a concentration of $3.000\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ was added. The resulting solution had a pH value of $\mathrm{pH} = 4.4246$.

The $^{1}$H-NMR of this acid is also available:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2024-3-fig1.png

The peak at 2.2 ppm is a singlet, the two peaks at 2.6 and 2.8 ppm are triplets.

3.1 Calculate the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A}$ value of this acid and its molar mass.

3.2 Give the sum formula and structural formula of this acid. Justify your statements by calculation and NMR.

B. The second acidic problem

Maleic acid ((Z)-but-2-enedioic acid) is a solid, diprotic acid at room temperature. We are looking for the two $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A}$ values of this acid.

First, $20.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of this acid were dissolved in $1.000$ liters of water. This solution had a pH value of $\mathrm{pH} = 1.408$. Assume that in this experimental set-up only the first protolysis stage of maleic acid plays a role in the pH value.

3.3 Calculate $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A1}$.

In a second experiment, $10.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of solid sodium hydroxide was added to the prepared maleic acid solution. This solution had a pH value of $6.135$.

3.4 Berechnen Sie $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{A}_2}$. [German in the English paper: Calculate $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{A}_2}$.]

C. The third acidic problem

A diluted sulphuric acid solution of unknown concentration has a pH value of $\mathrm{pH} = 1.000$. We are looking for the molar concentrations of all sulphuric acid species in this solution. For the sake of simplicity, assume that the first protolysis of the sulphuric acid is complete. For sulphuric acid the acid constants are $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A1} = -3.00$ and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{A2} = 1.92$.

3.5 Calculate the concentrations of hydrogen sulphate and sulphate assuming that the first protolysis of the sulphuric acid is complete.

3.6 Check whether the assumption of complete protolysis was justified or not and calculate the sum of the concentrations of all sulphur-containing species in this solution.

Around 250000 tonnes of lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) are produced worldwide every year, which is mainly used in the food industry and for the production of polymers (polylactides, PLA). As a biocompatible and biodegradable plastic, PLA has numerous applications - from packaging materials to horticulture and medical technology. PLA is also one of the most commonly used materials in 3D printing.

However, PLA also has disadvantages such as low thermal stability, mainly due to its poor crystallization ability. In order to improve the properties of PLA, stereocomplex polylactic acids are therefore produced. Stereocomplex lactic acid (sc-PLA) is produced by mixing the two enantiomers of PLA and has a higher crystallization rate and a melting point approx. $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ higher than PLA. The gas pressure of the resulting ethine is used in the carbide method (CM) to determine the residual moisture of screed and wall samples. $50.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of the sample is placed in a steel bottle together with a glass ampoule containing calcium carbide and a few steel balls. Problem 6 (7 points). Kinetics with halogen compounds

Author: I. Stadler-Ulitsch

The following problem deals with various halogen compounds.

A. Sulfuryl chloride

Sulphuryl chloride is a colorless, high-density substance that corrodes in the presence of water and can serve as a starting material for aromatic sulphonic acid chlorides. At a certain temperature, $\ce{SO2Cl2}$ decomposes according to 1st order kinetics with $k = 2.81\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

6.1 Specify the half-life of the reaction.

6.2 Specify the period of time after which the concentration of $\ce{SO2Cl2}$ decreases to $10\,\%$ of the initial value.

B. Hydrogen chloride

The kinetics of the reaction

$$\ce{2 ICl_{(g)} + H2_{(g)} -> I2_{(g)} + 2 HCl_{(g)}} \qquad \text{R6.1}$$

were investigated and the following data were obtained:

$$\begin{array}{c|l|l|l} \text{Experiment} & [\ce{ICl}]_0\ /(\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}) & [\ce{H2}]_0\ /(\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}) & v_0\ /(\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 1 & 1.5 & 1.5 & 3.7\cdot10^{-7} \\ 2 & 3.0 & 1.5 & 7.4\cdot10^{-7} \\ 3 & 3.0 & 4.5 & 22\cdot10^{-7} \\ 4 & 4.7 & 2.7 & ? \end{array}$$

6.3 Determine the reaction orders in relation to ICl and $\ce{H2}$ and write down the differential rate law for R6.1.

6.4 Enter the rate constant for R6.1 in the correct unit and calculate the initial rate for experiment 4.

C. Benzendiazonium chloride

Benzendiazonium chloride is a strong, unstable electrophile. It can react with water, releasing $\ce{N2}$ to form phenol. The activation energy for this reaction is $99.1\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

6.5 Calculate the temperature at which the reaction rate is $10\,\%$ higher than at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

D. Oxygen difluoride

Oxygen difluoride is a colorless gas and one of the strongest oxidizing agents. It even reacts with xenon. It is thermally decomposed to fluorine and oxygen:

$$\ce{2 F2O_{(g)} -> 2 F2_{(g)} + O2_{(g)}}$$

The following rate law has been found experimentally:

$$-\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{F2O}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k_\mathrm{R}[\ce{F2O}]^2 + k'_\mathrm{R}[\ce{F2O}]^{\frac{3}{2}}$$

J. Czarnowski and H. J. Schumacher proposed the following reaction mechanism:

$$\begin{array}{lll} (1) & \ce{F2O + F2O -> F + OF + F2O} & k_\mathrm{a} \\ (2) & \ce{F + F2O -> F2 + OF} & k_\mathrm{b} \\ (3) & \ce{OF + OF -> O2 + F + F} & k_\mathrm{c} \\ (4) & \ce{F + F + F2O -> F2 + F2O} & k_\mathrm{d} \end{array}$$

Note: In (1), a molecule of a foreign gas X can also appear as a collision partner: $\ce{F2O + X -> F + OF + X}$. Here, however, we consider a situation in which only $\ce{F2O}$ occurs as a collision partner.

6.6 Using the steady-state model, show that this mechanism is consistent with the experimentally found rate law. Express the empirical constants $k_R$ and $k'_R$ by $k_{a\ldots d}$.

Problem 1 (5 points). Radioactive and Inorganic

Author: I. Stadler-Ulitsch

A. All About Radon

Radon is an invisible, odourless, radioactive noble gas. The air we breathe outdoors, indoors, and especially in underground caves contains a mixture of radon and its decay products. Radon thus contributes to the natural radiation exposure of humans and, due to its short-lived decay products, is responsible for approximately 10 % of all bronchial carcinomas.

The decisive nuclide is radon-222. It is produced by alpha decay from a parent nucleus, decays with a half-life of 3.8 days, and after several decays eventually forms lead-206.

1.1 State the number of $\alpha$ and $\beta^-$ decays between Rn-222 and Pb-206.

1.2 Write the equation for the formation of Rn-222 from its parent nucleus.

1.3 Calculate the mass of the Rn-222 atom, whose nuclear binding energy is $1714\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Give your result in atomic mass units (u) to three decimal places and show which values or constants you use.

In a residential space, the Rn-222 concentration resulted in an activity of $A = 50\,\mathrm{Bq}$ per cubic meter of air.

1.4 Calculate the number of Rn-222 atoms in one cubic meter of air.

Polonium-210 also belongs to the uranium-radium series and represents the actual health concern. It has a half-life of 138.4 days.

1.5 Calculate how long it takes for 85.5% of a given amount of $^{210}\mathrm{Po}$ to decay.

B. Inorganics from period 4

An important alloy of gallium with an element from a transition group (electron configuration …d$^3$…s$^2$) has a molar mass of $222.54\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ and is used as a superconductor with a critical temperature of $16.8\,\mathrm{K}$.

1.6 Give the empirical formula of the alloy.

In the 1990s the ability to produce high-quality GaN crystals via hydride vapor phase epitaxy led to the first commercially available blue LEDs. In the lab gallium nitride can be synthesized at $1050\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ from gallium and ammonia.

1.7 Provide a balanced equation for this synthesis of GaN.

Germanium was discovered in 1886 by the German chemist Clemens Winkler, who first noticed a deficit of 6.44% ($m/m$) among the components previously identified in argyrodite. As the name suggests, argyrodite contains silver as well as another element – but not lead – in a 4 : 3 ratio.

1.8 Provide the molar mass of argyrodite.

1.9 Give the empirical formula of argyrodite and show through calculation the agreement with the given data.

Germanium(IV) fluoride reacts with water to form Germanium(IV) oxide and hexafluorogermanic acid, in which the oxidation state of germanium remains unchanged.

1.10 Write a balanced equation for this reaction.

In contrast, when arsenic(III) oxide reacts with water, triprotic arsenious acid is formed. Passing hydrogen sulfide into a solution of this acid yields yellow orpiment ($246\,\mathrm{g/mol}$), a lemon-yellow compound that transforms into a red modification at $170\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, which sublimates well below its boiling point, forming dimers in the gas phase.

1.11 Write the balanced equation for the formation of arsenious acid.

1.12 Write the balanced equation for the synthesis of yellow orpiment.

1.13 Write the formula of the molecules in the gas phase of the red modification.

C. Finally, a comparison

problems.problem:
Problem 2 (7 points). Χρῶμα

Author: N. Langer

Chromium has a density of $\rho = 7.14\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The atomic radius is $1.25\,\text{Å}$. Chromium crystallizes in a regular cubic system – either body-centered or face-centered.

2.1 Determine in which of the two lattice types chromium crystallizes an provide a transparent calculation supporting your conclusion

Razor blades are made from an iron-chromium alloy. $0.1331\,\mathrm{g}$ of such a blade was dissolved in diluted sulfuric acid, forming iron(II) and chromium(III) ions. In the resulting solution, the iron was titrated with permanganate solution ($c = 0.0205\,\mathrm{mol/L}$). Volume used: $20.08\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. The chromium ions did not react under these conditions.

2.2 Give balanced, indexed (ionic) equations for the dissolution of iron, the dissolution of chromium, and the titration reaction.

2.3 Calculate the mass fractions of iron and chromium in the alloy.

Metallic chromium coatings can be produced by electrolysis. An electrolytic cell was filled with $100\,\mathrm{L}$ of a solution containing $230\,\mathrm{g/L}$ of "anhydrous chromic acid" ($\ce{CrO3}$). Electrolysis was then carried out at a current of $1500\,\mathrm{A}$ for 10 hours. The chrome plated objects served as the cathode, while the anode remained unchanged. The mass increase at the cathode was $670\,\mathrm{g}$, and gases were formed at both the cathode and the anode.

2.4 Give the formulae of the gases formed.

2.5 Calculate the percentage current efficiency for the described process.

Compounds or ions of chromium exhibit a multicolored appearance (χρωμα – color). The standard reduction potentials can be clearly represented in a Latimer diagram (all data refer to $\mathrm{pH} = 0$):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-2-fig1.png

2.6 Calculate $x$ and $y$ using the diagram.

In analytical chemistry, the redox system dichromate/chromium(III) ($E^\circ(\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}/\ce{Cr^{3+}}) = +1.33\,\mathrm{V}$) is often used.

2.7 Calculate the change in potential when the pH value is increased by 1 ($T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$), assuming the chromium species concentrations remain constant.

In coordination chemistry, numerous chromium complexes are known, such as $\ce{K3[Cr(CN)6]}$, which absorbs light with $\lambda = 376\,\mathrm{nm}$.

2.8 State the name and the color of the compound.

2.9 Calculate the ligand field splitting $\Delta_0$ of the complex.

Hexaaquachromium(III) complexes exhibit a special type of structural isomerism. When anhydrous chromium(III) chloride is dissolved, the dark green triaquachromium(III) chloride trihydrate $\mathbf{1}$ is first formed, which transforms into a green isomer $\mathbf{2}$, then into a light blue-green $\mathbf{3}$, and finally into a violet $\mathbf{4}$. During this process, the electrical conductivity of the solution increases.

2.10 Write the formulae of compounds $\mathbf{1}$ to $\mathbf{4}$ and state the specific name of this type of isomerism.

problems.title: The Mohr Method
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (7 points). The Mohr Method

Author: W. Faber

The titration according to Mohr (Carl Friedrich Mohr, 1806 - 1879) is a method for determining the concentration of chloride and bromide ions. The solution to be analyzed is titrated with silver nitrate solution, whereby silver chloride or silver bromide precipitates are formed. Potassium chromate is used as an indicator. At the equivalence point, excess silver ions form a colored silver chromate precipitate, the formation of which indicates the end point of the titration.

The solubility products are given for this task:

$$\begin{aligned} K_\mathrm{sp}(\ce{AgBr}) &= 5.35\cdot10^{-13}\\ K_\mathrm{sp}(\ce{Ag2CrO4}) &= 1.12\cdot10^{-12}\\ K_\mathrm{sp}(\ce{AgOH}) &= 1.52\cdot10^{-8} \end{aligned}$$

$2.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a $\ce{K2CrO4}$ solution ($c = 0.3\,\mathrm{mol/L}$) are added to $50.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a sample solution with a bromide ion concentration of $0.200\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, the pH is adjusted to 7.00 by adding a buffer and the solution is made up to $100.00\,\mathrm{mL}$. This solution is titrated with a silver nitrate solution ($c = 0.100\,\mathrm{mol/L}$).

3.1 Calculate the maximum volume of silver nitrate solution that can be added before the first silver bromide precipitate forms. As this volume is probably very small, the change in volume of the solution in the titration flask can be neglected in this calculation.

For all further subtasks, it can be assumed that approximately all silver ions react with bromide ions as long as the bromide ions have not yet been consumed.

3.2 $60.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the silver nitrate solution are added to the sample solution. Calculate the concentration of bromide ions in this solution.

3.3 When $100.05\,\mathrm{mL}$ of silver nitrate solution is added, the equivalence point is just exceeded. Calculate the concentration of silver ions in this solution. Then show by calculation whether $\ce{Ag2CrO4}$ precipitate has already formed.

The pH value must be kept stable during this titration, as some of the chromate is converted into dichromate in an acidic solution. The so-called “chromate-dichromate equilibrium” is responsible for the pH dependency:

$$\ce{2 H+ + 2 CrO4^{2-} <=> Cr2O7^{2-} + H2O}\qquad K = 4.20\cdot10^{14}$$

Water as a solvent is not taken into account in the equilibrium constant.

3.4 Calculate what percentage of the chromate added before the titration is still present as chromate at the pH value of 7.00 before the start of the titration.

To increase the relative chromate concentration, it would be helpful to increase the pH value, but this could lead to the formation of silver hydroxide. Assume a silver ion concentration of $2.00\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$.

3.5 Calculate the pH value from which the formation of a silver hydroxide precipitate can be expected.

Problem 4 (12 points). Biochemistry and Organic Syntheses

Author: M. Scherl

A. Pathobiochemistry in metabolism: Phenylketonuria

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inherited metabolic disorder that impairs the processing of the amino acid phenylalanine $\mathbf{A}$. Without treatment, this accumulates in the body and can cause severe neurological damage. However, with early screening and a targeted diet, the disorder can be effectively controlled so that those affected can lead a largely normal life. Here are some metabolic pathways:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-4-fig1.png

• Reaction $\mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{F}$ is catalysed by a decarboxylase
• $\mathbf{F}$ is a neurotransmitter
• $\mathbf{X}$ is produced by hydroysis of $\mathbf{Y}$.
• The reaction $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{W} \to \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{X}$ requires an enzyme and a vitamin as a cofactor.
• $\mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{G}$ (a canonical amino acid) requires phenylalanine hydroxylase as an enzyme.

4.1 Draw the structures of $\mathbf{B}$ – $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$

4.2 Write down the correct enzyme class for the following reactions.

• $\mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{F}$
• $\mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{G}$
• $\mathbf{B} \to \mathbf{C}$
• $\mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{B}$

The conversion of $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{W} \to \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{X}$ takes place in several steps as a catalytic cycle, whereby this reaction sequence also occurs, in which one of the two starting materials (you have to decide which one) is converted:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-4-fig2.png

4.3 Name the circled functional group and draw the complete structure of “-OP” at physiological pH.

4.4 Draw the structures $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{K'}$ und $\mathbf{L}$.

B. Synthesis or Sapropterine

Sapropterin is a synthetic analog of tetrahydrobiopterin, an important co-factor for enzymes that break down phenylalanine. It is used to treat certain forms of phenylketonuria (PKU) in which residual phenylalanine hydroxylase activity is present. By taking it, the phenylalanine level in the blood can be lowered and the dietary requirements for PKU patients may be eased.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-4-fig3.png

• m-CPBA = meta-chloro perbenzoic acid
• Formation of $\mathbf{E}$: an additional heterocycle is formed.
• Formation of $\mathbf{F}$: the less stable double bound reacts.

4.5 Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{F}$ and the reagent $\mathbf{X}$ considering the correct stereochemistry.

C. The Poison of the Death Cap Mushroom – Amanitine

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-4-fig4.png

4.6 Circle all peptide bonds in the given structure. Indicate the number of amino acids in the present oligopeptide..

4.7 Label the canonical amino acids in the structure of amanitine with their names (3-letter abbreviation).

D. D. Farnesole - structure elucidation and synthesis

Farnesole was named after the Farnese acacia tree (Vachellia farnesiana) around 1905, as the substance was identified in the essence of its flowers. In this example, several paths - structure elucidation and synthesis - lead to the structure of farnesol.

Structure elucidation: Farnesole was subjected to ozonolysis and worked up with dimethyl sulphide. This yielded the three substances $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ in a ratio of 2 : 1 : 1..

A $^1\mathrm{H}$ and a $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ NMR spectrum of each of the three substances were recorded in $\ce{CD3OD}$.

$\mathbf{A}$: $\delta$ $^1\mathrm{H}$ [ppm]: 9.6, 1H (t, 6.65 Hz); 2.9, 2H (td, 7.41 Hz, 6.65 Hz); 2.7, 2H (t, 7.41 Hz); 2.1, 3H (s).

$\delta$ $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ [ppm]: 29.8; 35.6; 37.5; 200.0; 206.5.

$\mathbf{B}$: $\delta$ $^1\mathrm{H}$ [ppm]: 2.1, 6H (s)

$\delta$ $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ [ppm]: 30.7; 206.7.

$\mathbf{C}$: $\delta$ $^1\mathrm{H}$ [ppm]: 9.5, 1H (t, 6.03 Hz); 3.8, 2H (6.03 Hz).

$\delta$ $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ [ppm]: 63.9; 201.4.

In addition, farnesole was subjected to further chemical investigations to elucidate its structure:

• Reaction 1: Farnesole reacted with 3 equivalents of hydrogen
• Reaction 2: Farnesole reacted with ethanoic anhydride
• Reactions 3+4: Farnesole reacted with chromium(VI) oxide and the product with hydroxylamine.

4.8 Draw the structures of the ozonolysis producs $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$.

4.9 Draw the structural formulae of the reaction products for two of the four reactions and label them “reaction 1, 2, 3 or 4” accordingly.

Synthesis

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-4-fig5.png

• $\mathbf{C}$: a mass spectrum is given.
• $\mathbf{D}$ und $\mathbf{E}$ show signals in IR
• $\mathbf{D}$: a signal at $2260\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{E}$: a signal at $2155\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and a signal at $3300\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (broad).

4.10 Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{F}$ from this synthesis with the correct stereochemistry.

4.11 Draw the structure of farnsesole (including stereochemistry) and give the IUPAC-name.
