Problem 6 (4 points). Kinetics ABC

Author: I. Stadler-Ulitsch

The following reaction proceeds via an unknown mechanism:

$$\ce{A + 2 B -> AB2}.\qquad(\mathbf{R1})$$

Let us first assume that the reaction is second order with respect to B.

6.1 Select by checking the boxes those of the following mechanisms that would be consistent with this assumption.

• ☐ $\ce{A + B -> AB}$ slow; $\ce{AB + B -> AB2}$ fast
• ☐ $\ce{B + B -> B2}$ slow; $\ce{A + B2 -> AB2}$ fast
• ☐ $\ce{A + A -> A2}$ slow; $\ce{B + B -> B2}$ slow; $\ce{A2 + B2 -> AB2 + A}$ slow
• ☐ $\ce{A + B -> AB}$ fast; $\ce{AB + B -> AB2}$ slow

Diagrams are shown that can represent the relationship between [B] and time $t$ as well as the reaction rate $v$ and [B].

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-6-fig1.png

6.2 Write down the letters (a) to (f) of the diagrams that match the assumption made above. Assume a constant concentration for [A].

In reality, reaction $\mathbf{R1}$ proceeds via the following mechanism:

$$\begin{aligned} &\ce{A + B <=>[$k_1$][$k_{-1}$] AB} &&(1)\\ &\ce{AB + B ->[$k_2$] AB2} &&(2) \end{aligned}$$

6.3 For each of the conditions listed below, state the rate-determining step. Assume that [A] and [B] are much greater than [AB] and [$\mathrm{AB_2}$].

• $k_1 \gg k_{-1};\ k_2 \gg k_1$ ☐ Step1 ☐ Step2 ☐ neither of them
• $k_1 \gg k_{-1};\ k_2 \ll k_1$ ☐ Step1 ☐ Step2 ☐ neither of them
• $k_1 \gg k_{-1};\ k_2 \cong k_1$ ☐ Step1 ☐ Step2 ☐ neither of them
• $k_1 \cong k_{-1};\ k_2 \ll k_1$ ☐ Step1 ☐ Step2 ☐ neither of them

Unknown amounts of reagents A and B were placed together in a container under conditions that favor reaction 1. At time $t = t_1$, the concentration of the intermediate AB had become constant, $[\mathrm{AB}] = [\mathrm{AB}]_\mathrm{const}$, and the concentration of reagent A had reached a specific value, $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_1$.

6.4 At time $t_1$, express the ratio $k_1/k_2$ in terms of $[\mathrm{A}]_1$ and $[\mathrm{AB}]_\mathrm{const}$. Assume that $k_1, k_2 \gg k_{-1}$..

problems.title: Complexes of Copper(II) with Amino Acids
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (9 points). Complexes of Copper(II) with Amino Acids

Author: J. Novacek

Copper(II) ions form complexes with amino acids (HAS) with the molecular formula $\ce{[Cu(AS)2(H2O)]}$. These complexes usually crystallize as a monohydrate and are present as distorted octahedral complexes. For the sake of simplicity, they will be considered as square planar complexes for the following calculations and water will be ignored as a ligand (unless otherwise stated).

A. Analysis of copper(II)-bisglycinate

The reaction of copper(II) acetate with glycine produces two different products (complex cis-$\mathbf{I}$ and trans-$\mathbf{I}$). These cannot be analyzed by NMR due to the copper(II) ions, which is why the standard analysis method for these complexes is IR. The resulting spectra $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are shown on the page 23.

To assign the individual peaks to different vibrations, the compound is “labeled” with different isotopes (e.g. $^{13}\mathrm{C}$, $^{15}\mathrm{N}$, $^{18}\mathrm{O}$,...). It is then analyzed which peaks have shifted as a result (note: the force constant does not change significantly). This was done for the assignment of the signals of spectrum B.

To determine how well the labeling worked, an elemental analysis was carried out on both the unlabeled and the $^{18}\mathrm{O}$-labeled complex $\mathbf{I}$ (copper(II) bisglycinate monohydrate, $\ce{CuC4H10N2O5}$). The unlabeled complex had a carbon content of 20.9%, while the $^{18}\mathrm{O}$-labeled complex had a carbon content of 20.2%.

7.1 Calculate the relative amount of labeled oxygen atoms in the copper(II) bisglycinate monohydrate.

7.2 Which type of bond is responsible for each of the following signals in spectrum B?

• $3255\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$
• $2955\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$
• $1574\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$

7.3 Labeling the oxygen atoms with $^{18}\mathrm{O}$ causes some signals to shift significantly in the IR spectrum. Mark the correct statements with a cross:

The signal at $3255\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ is shifted

• ☐ to higher wave numbers.
• ☐ not significantly.
• ☐ to lower wave numbers.

The signal at $2955\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ is shifted

• ☐ to higher wave numbers.
• ☐ not significantly.
• ☐ to lower wave numbers.

The signal at $1574\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ is shifted

• ☐ to higher wave numbers.
• ☐ not significantly.
• ☐ to lower wave numbers.

The signal in spectra $\mathbf{B}$ at $475\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ corresponds to a Cu-N-vibration (those vibrations can be found between $450$-$500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), which is treated as harmonic oscillator.

7.4 Calculate the force constant $k$ of the Cu-N vibration.

7.5 Assign the IR spectra $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ to the corresponding complexes and give reasons for your assignment:

• cis-copper(II)-bisglycinate
• trans-copper(II)-bisglycinate

B. Chiral complexes of copper(II) with amino acids

The use of amino acids as ligands is not only advantageous due to the formation of chelate complexes, but also because chiral complexes are easily accessible - for example using alanine ((R)-2-aminopropanoic acid), proline ($\ce{C5H9NO2}$), leucine ($\ce{C6H13NO2}$), isoleucine ($\ce{C6H13NO2}$) and phenylalanine ($\ce{C9H11NO2}$).

One of these chiral complexes (complex $\mathbf{II}$) shows the following isotope pattern in MS:

$$\begin{array}{l|cccc} & \mathrm{M} & \mathrm{M+1} & \mathrm{M+2} & \mathrm{M+3} \\ \hline \text{Intensity} & 100 & 12 & 45 & 5 \end{array}$$

Natural abundance of isotopes:

$$\begin{array}{ll|ll} \mathrm{Cu} & \text{has 2 natural isotopes, main isotop: } A = 63\,\mathrm{u} & \mathrm{N} & {}^{14}\mathrm{N}\text{: } 99.6\%,\ {}^{15}\mathrm{N}\text{: } 0.4\% \\ \mathrm{C} & {}^{12}\mathrm{C}\text{: } 98.9\%,\ {}^{13}\mathrm{C}\text{: } 1.1\% & \mathrm{O,\ H} & \text{can be considered as pure isotopes for this task} \end{array}$$

C. Asymmetric synthesis with chiral copper(II)-complexes

While the synthesis of chiral complexes may be interesting and challenging in its own, the question of application often arises. Fortunately, copper salts and complexes have proven to be extremely helpful (and inexpensive) catalysts for a wide variety of reactions.

The simple ketone $\mathbf{K}$ is converted into enolates using the reactions below. Depending on the reagents and reaction conditions used, different products are formed (whereby a main isomer and a secondary isomer are formed in a ratio of ~4:1 in each case). Cy = cyclohexyl

Problem 8 (12 points). Bromine from a Physicochemical Point of View

Author: G. Schellander

The Phases

Shown is a phase diagram of bromine ($\ce{Br2}$), the axes are labelled but not to scale, as you will easily recognise.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/at-2025-8-fig1.png

8.1 Correctly assign the letters s, l and g, which are normally used in phase diagrams, to fields A-C.

8.2 Bromine is present in all three states of aggregation if... (tick the right box)

• ☐ $T < -7{,}3\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $p > 5{,}8\,\mathrm{kPa}$
• ☐ $T = -7{,}3\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $p = 101{,}3\,\mathrm{kPa}$
• ☐ $T = -7{,}3\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $p = 57{,}2\,\mathrm{matm}$
• ☐ $T = 7{,}3\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $p = 58\,\mathrm{kPa}$
